AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the finite element formulation for rotor-stator coupling in permanent magnet synchronous machines can be rigorously embedded into the HMDD framework, which gives it inherited well-posedness and error-estimate guarantees, and that the method is practically credible through comparison with an established iso-geometric analysis code.

title: Reducing the GPU Memory Bottleneck with Lossless Compression for ML -- Extended
comment: Extended version of paper published at 21st European Conference on Computer Systems (EUROSYS '26), April 27-30, 2026, Edinburgh, Scotland Uk
summary: Machine learning (ML) training and inference often process data sets far exceeding GPU memory capacity, forcing them to rely on PCIe for on-demand tensor transfers, causing critical transfer bottlenecks. Lossy compression has been proposed to relieve bottlenecks but introduces workload-dependent accuracy loss, making it complex or even prohibitive to use in existing ML deployments. We explore lossless compression as an alternative that avoids this deployment complexity. We identify where lossless compression can be integrated into ML pipelines while minimizing interference with GPU execution. Based on our findings, we introduce Invariant Bit Packing (IBP), a novel lossless compression algorithm designed to minimize data transfer time for ML. IBP identifies and eliminates invariant bits across groups of tensors, improving throughput through GPU-optimized decompression that leverages warp parallelism, low-overhead bit operations, and asynchronous PCIe transfers. We provide easy-to-use APIs, showcasing them by adding IBP support to GNN training, as well as DLRM and LLM inference frameworks. IBP achieves, on average, 74% faster GNN training, 180% faster DLRM embedding lookup, and 24% faster LLM inference.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes IBP, a lossless tensor compression method for ML data transfers that cuts PCIe bottlenecks without hurting accuracy, delivering substantial speedups across GNN, DLRM, and LLM workloads.
AI.motivation: Modern ML workloads often operate on datasets larger than GPU memory, forcing frequent PCIe tensor transfers that become a major bottleneck. Prior lossy compression approaches reduce traffic but create workload-specific accuracy concerns and deployment complexity, motivating a lossless alternative.
AI.method: The paper studies where lossless compression can be inserted into ML data pipelines with minimal GPU interference, then proposes Invariant Bit Packing (IBP), which removes invariant bits across tensor groups and uses GPU-optimized decompression with warp parallelism, lightweight bit operations, and asynchronous PCIe transfers.
AI.result: IBP is integrated into GNN training, DLRM inference, and LLM inference frameworks, achieving average speedups of 74% for GNN training, 180% for DLRM embedding lookup, and 24% for LLM inference.
AI.conclusion: IBP demonstrates that carefully integrated lossless compression can significantly reduce PCIe transfer bottlenecks in ML systems without introducing accuracy risks, making it practical for deployment across training and inference workloads.

title: Cross-Lingual Steering for Figurative Language Generation
summary: Multilingual large language models can generate figurative language, but whether the internal signals driving this behavior are language-specific or reusable across languages is unclear. Using activation steering as a probe, we estimate a direction for a figurative category from figurative--literal activation differences in one language and apply it during generation. Across five figurative categories, six languages, and four multilingual LLMs, these directions steer reliably within their own language, most robustly for metaphor and simile. More importantly, they transfer across languages: a direction learned in one increases the target behavior when applied to another, with German among the most receptive targets. Going further, directions assembled from other languages can match or even surpass a target language's own native direction, while removing this shared component weakens native steering. Together, these results provide direct evidence of a reusable but target-dependent cross-lingual signal for figurative generation.

AI.tldr: Activation-steering experiments show that multilingual LLMs use a shared but target-dependent cross-lingual signal for generating figurative language, with strong evidence from transfer across languages and figurative categories.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand whether the internal mechanisms that support figurative language generation in multilingual LLMs are language-specific or shared across languages. This addresses a core question about cross-lingual representation reuse in multilingual models.
AI.method: The authors use activation steering as a probing method. They compute steering directions from activation differences between figurative and literal examples in one language, then inject these directions during generation and test both within-language and cross-lingual transfer across five figurative categories, six languages, and four multilingual LLMs.
AI.result: The results show that steering directions work reliably within the source language, especially for metaphor and simile, and also transfer across languages. German is reported as a particularly receptive target. In some cases, directions composed from other languages match or outperform a target language's native direction, while removing the shared component reduces native steering effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that multilingual LLMs contain a reusable cross-lingual internal signal for figurative language generation. This signal is not fully language-specific: directions learned from one language can steer figurative generation in another, although transfer strength depends on the target language.

title: Mitigating Content Shift and Hallucination in GenAI Image Editing via Structural Refinement
summary: Generative AI (GenAI) image editors, such as Nano Banana, produce visually compelling results for retouching tasks, enabling non-experts to edit images through text prompts alone. However, the generative nature of these models often introduces spatial misalignment, texture distortion, and content hallucination, all of which are detrimental to downstream workflows that require pixel-level fidelity. We identify a problem setting we call "structure-preserving GenAI fusion" for black-box GenAI image retouching: retain the perceptual enhancements of a GenAI output while enforcing structural faithfulness to the original input image. To address this problem, we propose a post-processing framework that fuses an input image with its GenAI-enhanced counterpart by first establishing coarse spatial and photometric correspondences, then performing a fusion stage that transfers desired enhancements while suppressing hallucinated content. In the absence of direct prior work in this setting, we evaluate our framework against representative methods from photorealistic style transfer and image fusion. Our experiments demonstrate that our method better preserves aesthetic quality while maintaining pixel-level structural consistency and the input resolution.

AI.tldr: A black-box post-processing fusion method combines the original image with a GenAI-edited version so users keep the nice visual edits but avoid misalignment and hallucinated details; it works better than existing style-transfer and fusion baselines.
AI.motivation: Current GenAI image editors produce appealing retouching results for non-experts, but their generative behavior often causes spatial misalignment, texture distortion, and hallucinated content, which makes them unsuitable for workflows requiring exact structural consistency.
AI.method: The method first estimates coarse spatial and photometric correspondences between the original image and the GenAI-retouched output, then performs a fusion stage that transfers desirable retouching effects while suppressing hallucinated or structurally inconsistent content.
AI.result: Experiments show the proposed framework outperforms representative photorealistic style transfer and image fusion methods in balancing aesthetic enhancement with pixel-level structural consistency, while also preserving the input resolution.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that a post-processing fusion framework can preserve the perceptual improvements from black-box GenAI image retouching while restoring pixel-level structural fidelity and original resolution better than representative style transfer and image fusion baselines.

title: Procedural Generation of First Person Shooter Maps using Map-Elites
summary: We investigate the application of MAP-Elites (a well-known quality diversity algorithm) to design levels for First-Person Shooter (FPS) games. We consider two well-known map representations (All-Black and Grid-Graph) and introduce two novel representations (Point-Line and Spatial-Layout) that improve the characterization of FPS maps. We define a series of metrics to describe maps' topological properties (which solely depend on maps' layout), and emergent properties (which must be evaluated through actual gameplay). We perform an in-depth analysis to identify the most suitable features to guide MAP-Elites illumination process. We apply MAP-Elites with Sliding Boundaries (MESB) to evolve populations of FPS maps. Our results show that the new representations can generate maps with higher diversity and quality than the representations previously used for evolving FPS maps.

AI.tldr: The paper uses MAP-Elites to generate FPS maps, introduces two better map representations, and shows they create more diverse and higher-quality maps than older methods.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to improve procedural generation of FPS maps by finding better map representations and feature descriptors that allow quality-diversity algorithms such as MAP-Elites to generate levels that are both varied and high quality.
AI.method: The paper applies the MAP-Elites quality-diversity algorithm, specifically MAP-Elites with Sliding Boundaries (MESB), to evolve FPS game maps. It compares four map representations: two existing ones (All-Black and Grid-Graph) and two new ones (Point-Line and Spatial-Layout). It also defines topological and emergent gameplay metrics and analyzes which features are most suitable for guiding the illumination process.
AI.result: The results show that the newly introduced Point-Line and Spatial-Layout representations produce FPS maps with higher diversity and quality than previously used representations. The study also identifies useful topological and emergent features for guiding MAP-Elites.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that applying MAP-Elites with Sliding Boundaries to FPS level generation is effective, and that the two newly proposed map representations, Point-Line and Spatial-Layout, outperform older representations in producing maps with better quality and greater diversity.

title: When LLMs Learn to Be Consistently Wrong: A Multi-Model Study of Linear Representations of Synthetic Deception
summary: Deceptive alignment, in which models maintain accurate internal representations while deliberately producing false outputs, remains a central challenge in AI safety. While strategic deception is the primary long-term concern, synthetic dishonesty - induced via direct optimization on incorrect answers - provides a controlled testbed for studying the representational basis of learned deception. We introduce a multi-model paradigm in which honest and deceptive variants of five transformer models (Pythia-1.4B, Gemma-2-2B/9B, Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B) are fine-tuned using LoRA on the same question distribution. Linear probes trained on mean-pooled hidden states detect synthetic dishonesty with near-perfect AUC (greater than or equal to 0.99) as early as layers 1-3 in four architectures, while Pythia-1.4B reaches a peak of 0.705. Logistic regression probes consistently match or outperform MLP probes, supporting the Linear Representation Hypothesis. Probes trained on TruthfulQA generalize with near-zero loss (Delta AUC approx. 0) to held-out MMLU subjects. Late-layer representations show strong robustness to Gaussian noise, with Gemma-2 models exhibiting exceptional stability. Mechanistic analysis of Fisher Discriminant Ratio, effective rank, centroid geometry, directional stability, cross-domain alignment, and calibration (ECE) reveals two regimes: representational collapse in Pythia/Llama/Qwen versus high-dimensional preservation in Gemma-2. Across all models, the dishonesty direction consolidates progressively in deeper layers, with optimal calibration (ECE less than 0.01 except Pythia) achievable in layers 1-4. These results demonstrate that robust, domain-invariant dishonesty representations can be rapidly entrenched via modest supervised fine-tuning, with implications for activation-based monitoring.

AI.tldr: By fine-tuning models to answer dishonestly, the paper shows that deception-like internal representations emerge quickly, are easy to detect with simple linear probes, generalize across domains, and differ by architecture, with Gemma-2 showing the strongest and most stable high-dimensional dishonesty structure.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to study the representational basis of learned deception in a controlled setting. Since strategic deception is hard to isolate directly, the paper uses synthetic dishonesty induced by supervised optimization on wrong answers as an experimentally tractable proxy for deceptive alignment concerns in AI safety.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune honest and deceptive variants of five transformer models using LoRA on the same question distribution, then train linear and MLP probes on mean-pooled hidden states across layers to detect dishonesty. They evaluate transfer from TruthfulQA to held-out MMLU subjects and analyze representation geometry, robustness, alignment, and calibration using metrics such as AUC, Fisher Discriminant Ratio, effective rank, centroid geometry, directional stability, and ECE.
AI.result: Linear probes achieve near-perfect detection performance (AUC >= 0.99) from layers 1-3 in four of five architectures, while Pythia-1.4B performs much worse with a peak AUC of 0.705. Logistic regression matches or outperforms MLP probes, transfer across domains incurs almost no loss, late layers are robust to Gaussian noise, Gemma-2 is especially stable, and calibration is excellent in early layers for most models.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that synthetic dishonesty can be encoded as a robust, domain-invariant internal representation after modest supervised fine-tuning, and that this signal is detectable very early in transformer layers with simple linear probes. It also finds architecture-dependent representational regimes, with Gemma-2 preserving higher-dimensional structure and stronger robustness than Pythia, Llama, and Qwen.

title: Forecasting threshold exceedance of atmospheric variables at a specific location
summary: This study compares two methodological approaches for predicting, at a given site, threshold exceedances of atmospheric variables such as temperature and wind speed: (i) direct probabilistic methods, which treat exceedance as a binary classification problem, and (ii) full distribution probabilistic methods, which model the complete conditional probability law of the target variable. Using theoretical analysis and numerical simulations on a toy model, alongside real-world data from the MeteoNet dataset (2016--2018) for southeastern France, we demonstrate that the full distribution approach consistently outperforms the direct method for rare, extreme events. This advantage arises because the full distribution approach effectively learns the parameters of the conditional distribution from moderate and mild intensity events, thereby achieving better calibration and discrimination in the tails. We find that the specific parametric shape of the chosen distribution plays a secondary role compared to accurately capturing predictable shifts in its bulk properties (i.e., mean and variance). This empirical indistinguishability is also informative about the physical mechanics driving atmospheric extremes, suggesting that extreme exceedances are primarily driven by significant conditional displacements of the entire distribution rather than by unpredictable, fat-tailed anomalies within a static climatology. Our results are validated for both strong surface wind speeds and intense hourly rainfall, with performance evaluated using proper scoring rules (Brier score, logarithmic score) and deterministic skill scores (Peirce Skill Score, CSI, HSS). These findings highlight the critical importance of modeling the full probability distribution for rare-event forecasting and provide practical guidance for improving extreme weather prediction in operational meteorology.

AI.tldr: Forecast the whole weather-variable distribution, not just exceedance yes/no: it gives better rare-event predictions because it learns distribution shifts from common events and improves tail forecasts.
AI.motivation: Rare extreme weather events are difficult to predict reliably. The study aims to determine whether forecasting threshold exceedances is better handled directly as a classification task or indirectly through modeling the full distribution of the target variable.
AI.method: The paper compares two probabilistic forecasting approaches: direct binary exceedance prediction and full conditional distribution modeling. It uses theoretical analysis, toy-model simulations, and MeteoNet real-world data from southeastern France (2016–2018), evaluating performance with proper scoring rules and deterministic skill scores.
AI.result: The full distribution approach consistently outperforms the direct method for rare extremes in both calibration and discrimination. The main gain comes from learning predictable shifts in mean and variance from moderate events, while the exact parametric tail shape is less important.
AI.conclusion: Modeling the full conditional probability distribution of atmospheric variables yields more accurate forecasts of rare threshold exceedances than direct binary exceedance classification, especially for extreme events.

title: On limitations of polyconvexity
summary: Polyconvex constitutive modeling is attractive as it guarantees stability of numerical simulations and can improve the generalization behavior of material models. However, in certain applications, polyconvex formulations perform poorly in reproducing the underlying ground truth material response, which can effectively preclude their practical use. In this work, we address this issue and investigate the limitations of polyconvex constitutive modeling. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: (1) We analyze the theoretical reasons why polyconvexity may, in some cases, impose overly restrictive constraints that limit the achievable accuracy of constitutive models. Thereby, we provide analytical ellipticity guarantees for two non-polyconvex Mooney-Rivlin type potentials. (2) We investigate the practical limitations of polyconvex physics-augmented neural network constitutive models using two representative formulations: models using structural tensor-based invariants and models using signed singular values. Their performance is evaluated on datasets obtained from homogenized microstructured materials, and their predictive capabilities are assessed in finite element simulations. (3) Overall, we provide an overview of benefits, limitations, and mitigation strategies of polyconvex constitutive modeling.

AI.tldr: Polyconvex models are stable but can be too restrictive; this paper explains why, proves ellipticity for some non-polyconvex alternatives, tests polyconvex neural constitutive models, and summarizes when polyconvexity helps, hurts, and how to mitigate its drawbacks.
AI.motivation: Although polyconvex formulations guarantee numerical stability and often improve generalization, they can fail to reproduce the true constitutive response in some applications. This practical mismatch motivates a closer investigation into when and why polyconvexity becomes too restrictive.
AI.method: The paper combines theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation. It studies why polyconvexity can overly constrain constitutive models, derives analytical ellipticity guarantees for two non-polyconvex Mooney-Rivlin-type potentials, and evaluates two polyconvex physics-augmented neural network constitutive formulations on homogenized microstructured-material datasets and in finite element simulations.
AI.result: The study shows both theoretically and practically that polyconvexity may limit achievable model accuracy. It also demonstrates that certain non-polyconvex formulations can still admit analytical ellipticity guarantees, and it characterizes the performance limits of representative polyconvex neural constitutive models on benchmark datasets and FE simulations.
AI.conclusion: Polyconvex constitutive modeling offers stability and generalization advantages, but its constraints can be too restrictive and may reduce accuracy for some material responses. The paper concludes that polyconvexity is beneficial but not universally appropriate, and its limitations should be mitigated through informed modeling strategies.

title: Federated Variational Preference Alignment with Gumbel-Softmax Prior for Personalized User Preferences
summary: Federated Learning (FL) offers a privacy-preserving pathway for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs); however, existing frameworks typically enforce a monolithic reward model, inevitably averaging out inherently conflicting user preferences (e.g., helpfulness vs. harmlessness). While Variational Preference Learning (VPL) offers a pathway to personalization, adapting it to decentralized settings presents a fundamental challenge: posterior collapse driven by severe local data scarcity and heterogeneity. In this paper, we propose Federated Variational Preference Alignment with Gumbel-Softmax Prior (FedVPA-GP), a framework designed to disentangle diverse preferences without compromising privacy. To stabilize variational inference, we introduce a Federated Mixture Prior that enables clients to leverage the aggregate population distribution as a dynamic prior. Furthermore, we incorporate an Orthogonal Loss that explicitly enforces the separation of preference prototypes in the latent space. Experiments on the HH-RLHF dataset demonstrate that FedVPA-GP significantly outperforms monolithic baselines, successfully disentangling conflicting user intents and enabling dynamic preference switching.

AI.tldr: A federated framework for personalized LLM preference alignment that avoids posterior collapse with a federated mixture prior and orthogonal prototype separation, achieving better preference disentanglement and control than single-reward baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing federated LLM alignment methods rely on a single monolithic reward model, which averages out conflicting user preferences. Although variational preference learning suggests a route to personalization, applying it in federated settings is difficult because local data scarcity and heterogeneity cause posterior collapse.
AI.method: The paper proposes FedVPA-GP, a federated variational preference alignment framework using a Gumbel-Softmax-based latent preference formulation, a Federated Mixture Prior to stabilize decentralized variational inference under scarce and heterogeneous local data, and an Orthogonal Loss to separate latent preference prototypes.
AI.result: On the HH-RLHF dataset, FedVPA-GP significantly outperforms monolithic baselines, better disentangles diverse and conflicting user intents, and enables controllable switching among preferences.
AI.conclusion: FedVPA-GP can disentangle conflicting user preferences in federated LLM alignment while preserving privacy, outperforming monolithic reward-model baselines and supporting dynamic preference switching.

title: Dex2HOI: Dexterous Bimanual Two-Object Interaction Generation
summary: Recent advances in 4D Human-Object Interaction (HOI) generation have enabled increasingly realistic motion synthesis, particularly for single-object manipulation. Yet current research overlooks an inherent property of human behavior: people naturally coordinate both hands and manipulate multiple objects simultaneously. To address this gap, we present Dex2HOI, a unified diffusion model for single- and two-object HOI synthesis from text. At its core, Dex2HOI employs a Dual-Stream Diffusion approach, where each object is processed in a dedicated interaction stream and coordinated through bidirectional cross-attention. To synthesize the final motion, we introduce a Motion Fusion Network integrated with novel hand-relative object representations and contact-aware conditioning applied across the whole sequence. By sampling the diffusion process autoregressively over prefix-conditioned windows, Dex2HOI generates arbitrarily long sequences at real-time speed omitting redundant test-time optimization, achieving up to x540 inference speed-up over prior state-of-the-art methods. Extensive evaluation on both single- and two-object benchmarks demonstrates state-of-the-art quantitative results, marking a step beyond conventional single-object HOI generation and toward expressive multi-object manipulation. Code and models will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: Dex2HOI is a unified diffusion model that generates long, real-time text-driven 4D HOI motions for one or two objects by coordinating dual interaction streams and fusing them into contact-aware bimanual motion, achieving SOTA accuracy and up to 540x faster inference.
AI.motivation: Existing 4D HOI generation methods mainly focus on single-object manipulation, but real human behavior often involves both hands and multiple objects used simultaneously. The work aims to close this gap by building a model that can synthesize richer, more natural multi-object interactions from text.
AI.method: The paper proposes Dex2HOI, a unified text-to-HOI diffusion model. It uses a Dual-Stream Diffusion architecture with one interaction stream per object and bidirectional cross-attention for coordination. A Motion Fusion Network combines the streams using hand-relative object representations and contact-aware conditioning over the full sequence. Long motions are generated autoregressively with prefix-conditioned windows, enabling real-time synthesis without redundant test-time optimization.
AI.result: Dex2HOI achieves state-of-the-art quantitative performance on both single-object and two-object benchmarks. It also delivers real-time long-sequence generation and reports up to 540x inference speed-up compared with prior state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.conclusion: Dex2HOI demonstrates that a unified diffusion framework can effectively generate both single-object and two-object 4D human-object interactions from text, advancing HOI generation toward realistic multi-object, bimanual manipulation with state-of-the-art accuracy and much faster inference.

title: Uncertainty-Aware and Temporally Regulated Expert Advice in Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Driving
comment: Accepted in The IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC) September 15-18, 2026 -- Naples, Italy
summary: Exploration in reinforcement learning for autonomous driving is inherently unsafe: agents must experience novel behaviors to learn, yet exploration can lead to collisions or off-road driving. We propose an uncertainty-aware framework that leverages expert advice to guide exploration while avoiding long-term dependence. Advice is triggered when epistemic or aleatoric uncertainty exceeds adaptive thresholds derived from rolling buffers, ensuring advice evolves with the agent's confidence. A commitment-cooldown strategy with a stochastic early-stop heuristic regulates the duration and frequency of guidance, exposing the agent to coherent maneuvers without exhausting the advice budget. Expert and agent experiences are combined in a shared replay buffer within an off-policy implicit quantile network (IQN) backbone, enabling efficient reuse of expert trajectories. Experiments in CARLA show that our method outperforms the IQN baseline, improving success by 5-7% and reducing failures, demonstrating that risk-sensitive uncertainty coupled with regulated expert integration enables safer and more efficient exploration for sensor-based RL policy learning in unsignalized intersection navigation.

AI.tldr: The paper adds uncertainty-triggered, carefully limited expert intervention to IQN-based RL for autonomous driving, improving safety and task success during exploration in CARLA.
AI.motivation: Exploration in autonomous-driving RL is unsafe because agents must try novel behaviors to learn, but this can cause collisions or off-road failures. The goal is to improve exploration safety without creating long-term dependence on expert guidance.
AI.method: The paper proposes an off-policy IQN-based RL framework that triggers expert advice when epistemic or aleatoric uncertainty exceeds adaptive thresholds from rolling buffers. A commitment-cooldown mechanism with stochastic early stopping controls how long and how often advice is used. Expert and agent data are stored in a shared replay buffer for efficient reuse.
AI.result: In CARLA experiments, the method outperforms the IQN baseline, increasing success rates by 5-7% and reducing failure cases, showing safer and more efficient learning.
AI.conclusion: An uncertainty-aware expert-advice framework can make reinforcement learning exploration for autonomous driving safer and more efficient, outperforming a standard IQN baseline in unsignalized intersection navigation.

title: LLMs Without Deep Neural Networks: New Architecture, Benefits and Case Study
summary: The purpose of this article is to provide validation to my deep neural network alternative in the context of LLMs. Very recently, there has been a significant interest by Chinese researchers in a model called RBF network, as a substitute to standard DNNs, with increased explainability and higher accuracy. It turns out that my new model, discovered independently, is based on the exact same machinery. But with a major twist: it does not need DNN as it finds the global optimum of the loss function in closed form, in one iteration, thus eliminating the tedious training step. Here I provide a high-level overview of my technology, with case study and comparison to similar methods.

title: When Certainty Is Not Worth It: Capital Lock-Up and Settlement Discounting in Prediction Markets
summary: Collateralized prediction markets are contingent-claim markets in which economic uncertainty can disappear before winning claims become redeemable. This paper studies the pricing effect of that delay. When collateral remains locked until oracle settlement, a near-certain dollar is a delayed dollar, so prices embed a maturity-dependent settlement discount in addition to beliefs about outcomes. We recover an implied settlement-discount term structure from persistent near-certain contracts using realized settlement times and summarize it as an annualized settlement wedge (ASW). The recovered wedges are positive, maturity-dependent, and time-varying. Adjusting pricesby these curves reduces the near-certainty horizon gradient by roughly 48-88%, indicating that much of the raw maturity pattern reflects priced settlement frictions rather than forecast error alone. Market architecture changes the wedge: negRisk conversion compresses discounts by recycling part of the position into synthetic collateral, while yield-bearing collateral flattens the term structure by reducing the opportunity cost of lock-up. The results show that pricing quality in prediction markets is endogenous to settlement mechanics, collateral productivity, and capital-recycling design. Prediction-market prices therefore aggregate information through a financial infrastructure whose funding conditions are measurable and economically important.

AI.tldr: Delayed redemption in collateralized prediction markets creates a measurable settlement discount. By estimating this discount from near-certain contracts, the paper shows that much of the apparent maturity-related mispricing is actually due to settlement mechanics and collateral design, not just forecasting error.
AI.motivation: The motivation is that in collateralized prediction markets, uncertainty about the event outcome may effectively disappear before the winning claim becomes redeemable because collateral stays locked until oracle settlement. This creates a potential gap between prices and beliefs: even a near-certain payoff may trade below one dollar because settlement is delayed. The paper aims to isolate and quantify this settlement-friction component of prices.
AI.method: The authors infer an implied settlement-discount term structure from persistent near-certain contracts by combining observed prices with realized settlement times. They summarize this term structure using an annualized settlement wedge (ASW) and then evaluate how adjusting market prices by the recovered discount curves changes the observed horizon gradient in near-certain contracts. They also compare wedges across different market-architecture features, including negRisk conversion and yield-bearing collateral.
AI.result: The paper finds positive, maturity-dependent, and time-varying settlement wedges. After adjusting prices using the estimated settlement-discount curves, the near-certainty horizon gradient falls by about 48–88%, implying that much of the raw maturity effect comes from settlement frictions. It also finds that negRisk conversion compresses the discount and that yield-bearing collateral flattens the term structure by lowering the opportunity cost of locked collateral.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that prediction-market prices are materially shaped by settlement delay and collateral mechanics. A substantial part of the maturity-related pricing pattern in near-certain contracts reflects a priced settlement discount rather than pure belief distortion, and this discount can be measured, varies with maturity and time, and is altered by market design choices such as negRisk conversion and yield-bearing collateral.

title: DG-CoLearn: An Efficient Collaborative Learning Framework for Dynamic Graphs
summary: Dynamic graph learning (DGL) is essential for modelling evolving graph data, but existing methods suffer from significant computational overhead due to repeated full-snapshot retraining and are not well-suited for collaborative settings with partitioned data. In realistic graph systems, cross-partition edges are unavoidable, but direct sharing of graph structure between clients may violate privacy constraints. We propose DG-CoLearn, a client-oblivious collaborative dynamic graph learning framework built on incremental graph snapshot processing, which focuses computation on graph regions affected by temporal updates while preserving historical information through temporal modelling. This incremental design is consistently applied across the entire graph processing pipeline, including a server-mediated embedding exchange mechanism to enable accurate multi-hop message passing without exposing raw cross-client structural information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DG-CoLearn achieves up to 33.8$\times$ speedup in training time and 27.4$\times$ reduction in communication overhead, while consistently improving predictive performance on both node classification (up to 13.36% F1 improvement) and link prediction (up to 8.27% MAP improvement) tasks. These results highlight the effectiveness of DG-CoLearn in bridging efficiency, scalability, and client-to-client structural privacy in collaborative dynamic graph learning.

AI.tldr: DG-CoLearn is an incremental and privacy-preserving collaborative dynamic graph learning framework that updates only changed graph regions and exchanges embeddings instead of raw structure, yielding large gains in speed, communication efficiency, and prediction quality.
AI.motivation: Existing dynamic graph learning methods are inefficient because they repeatedly retrain on full graph snapshots, causing high computational cost. They also do not fit collaborative settings well, where graph data is partitioned across clients and cross-partition edges exist. Directly sharing graph structure in such settings can violate privacy constraints, motivating a framework that is efficient, scalable, and privacy-preserving.
AI.method: The paper proposes DG-CoLearn, a client-oblivious collaborative dynamic graph learning framework. Its core method is incremental graph snapshot processing that updates only graph regions affected by temporal changes while retaining historical information through temporal modelling. The framework applies this incremental strategy across the full pipeline and uses a server-mediated embedding exchange mechanism so clients can perform accurate multi-hop message passing across partitions without directly sharing raw structural data.
AI.result: Experiments show that DG-CoLearn achieves up to 33.8x training speedup and 27.4x communication overhead reduction. It also improves predictive performance consistently on node classification and link prediction, with up to 13.36% F1 improvement and 8.27% MAP improvement, respectively.
AI.conclusion: DG-CoLearn effectively improves collaborative dynamic graph learning by combining incremental snapshot processing with privacy-preserving cross-client embedding exchange, achieving better efficiency, lower communication cost, and stronger predictive performance without exposing raw cross-client graph structure.

title: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced Zero-Shot Topic Classification: A Multi-Strategy Comparative Study
comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, ACL format. This paper proposes a KG-augmented zero-shot multi-label topic classification framework and evaluates multiple strategies
summary: Multi-label topic classification without labeled training data is a challenging task, specially when documents contain complex relational information. We present a zero-shot multi-label topic classification framework and systematically investigate how per-article knowledge graph augmentation affects its performance. The base framework classifies topics in documents without labeled training data and has four variants: article-only classification, keyword-enhanced classification, and self-consistency decoding variants of both. Then, we augment each base variant with per article knowledge graph. This graph is extracted from the input document through a pipeline similar to KGGen based on subject-predicate-object triples. We test all eight methods, four base and four graph augmented on fifteen LLMs and eight multi-label datasets across different domains. For the base framework, keyword-enhanced classification (AK) is the best performing method, and six out of fifteen LLMs surpass the sentence-encoder baseline. Graph augmentation has positive and negative impacts on small and large models, respectively. This shows that larger models already contain enough relational information from pretraining. Furthermore, the self-consistency decoding variant does not show performance improvements in any experiment while increasing computation costs about fivefold.

AI.tldr: The paper studies zero-shot multi-label topic classification with and without per-document knowledge graphs. Keyword enhancement is the strongest base approach, knowledge graphs mainly help smaller LLMs, larger LLMs often do not benefit, and self-consistency decoding is too expensive for no gain.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot multi-label topic classification is difficult without labeled training data, especially for documents containing complex relational information. The paper is motivated by the question of whether document-specific knowledge graph augmentation can improve LLM performance in this setting.
AI.method: The paper proposes a zero-shot multi-label topic classification framework with four base variants: article-only, keyword-enhanced, and self-consistency versions of both. Each variant is further augmented with a per-article knowledge graph extracted from the document using subject-predicate-object triples through a KGGen-like pipeline. The authors evaluate eight total methods on 15 LLMs and 8 multi-label datasets across domains.
AI.result: Among base methods, keyword-enhanced classification performs best, and 6 of 15 LLMs outperform a sentence-encoder baseline. Knowledge graph augmentation has mixed effects: positive for small models and negative for large models. Self-consistency decoding does not improve performance in any experiment and substantially increases computation cost.
AI.conclusion: Per-article knowledge graph augmentation helps smaller LLMs in zero-shot multi-label topic classification but tends to hurt larger LLMs, suggesting larger models already encode sufficient relational knowledge; self-consistency decoding is not worthwhile because it increases cost about fivefold without improving performance.

title: Clustering Guided Domain-Specific Pretrained Foundation Model Very High-Resolution Arctic Remote Sensing
summary: This study introduces a novel Arctic-focused remote sensing foundation model (RSFM) by combining diversity-aware regional-scale image curation with masked autoencoder (MAE) self-supervised pretraining of a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder for very-high-spatial-resolution (VHSR) satellite image analysis. Spectral and acquisition-metadata descriptors were used in a scalable affinity-propagation clustering workflow to select approximately 3 million chips from 267 TB of Vantor VHSR imagery This curation strategy was designed to reduce oversampling of visually repetitive or low-information areas while preserving broad scene diversity across the study domain. We pretrained a ViT-Large encoder on the curated corpus using a domain-adapted MAE reconstruction objective, producing Arctic-specific transformer weights for downstream feature mapping. The pretrained encoder was integrated into an existing location-aware detection and segmentation framework and evaluated across four hand-labeled Arctic datasets. Compared to ImageNet-initialized ViT-Large baseline, Arctic MAE pretraining produced consistent improvements in foreground mean F1 scores of 0.87, 0.72, 0.93, and 0.87, for infrastructure, IWP, RTS, and TCNs, with approximately 5-8 percentage increase. The proposed model also outperformed Prithvi-EO-2.0 in all downstream comparisons, with the smallest gain corresponding to at least a 15 percentage improvement mean F1, suggesting that domain-specific self-supervised pretraining on curated Arctic VHSR imagery provides more transferable representations for fine-scale Arctic mapping than a general-purpose Earth observation foundation model. These results demonstrate that optimizing the pretraining data distribution at regional scale, while keeping the architecture and MAE objective fixed, can produce a reusable Arctic-domain encoder for multiple VHSR remote sensing applications.

AI.tldr: A curated, Arctic-specific MAE-pretrained ViT-Large beats ImageNet and Prithvi-EO-2.0 for multiple Arctic VHSR mapping tasks, showing that region-specific data curation matters as much as scale for transferable remote-sensing representations.
AI.motivation: The motivation is that existing general-purpose foundation models and naive large-scale data sampling may not capture the fine-scale, region-specific characteristics of Arctic very-high-resolution imagery, so optimizing the pretraining data distribution for Arctic scenes could produce more transferable representations for Arctic mapping tasks.
AI.method: The method builds an Arctic-focused remote sensing foundation model by first curating about 3 million diverse image chips from 267 TB of Vantor VHSR imagery using spectral and acquisition-metadata descriptors with affinity-propagation clustering, then pretraining a ViT-Large encoder with a domain-adapted masked autoencoder objective, and finally integrating the pretrained encoder into a location-aware detection and segmentation framework for evaluation on four labeled Arctic datasets.
AI.result: Arctic MAE pretraining improved foreground mean F1 scores to 0.87, 0.72, 0.93, and 0.87 on infrastructure, IWP, RTS, and TCN tasks, corresponding to about 5–8 percentage-point gains over an ImageNet-initialized ViT-Large baseline, and it also outperformed Prithvi-EO-2.0 on all downstream tasks with the smallest gain still at least 15 percentage points in mean F1.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that domain-specific self-supervised pretraining on a curated Arctic VHSR satellite corpus yields a reusable Arctic remote sensing encoder that consistently improves downstream detection and segmentation performance over both ImageNet initialization and a general-purpose EO foundation model, even when the architecture and MAE objective remain fixed.

title: Harness Updating Is Not Harness Benefit: Disentangling Evolution Capabilities in Self-Evolving LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents are increasingly deployed as systems built around editable external harnesses, including prompts, skills, memories and tools, that shape task execution without changing model parameters. Harness self-evolution adapts such agents by updating these harnesses from execution evidence. Yet it remains unclear whether a model's base capability in task-solving predicts its capabilities in harness self-evolution: which models produce useful harness updates, and which actually benefit from them? We analyze two harness self-evolution capabilities: (i) harness-updating, the capability to produce useful persistent harness updates from execution evidence; (ii) harness-benefit, the capability to benefit from updated harnesses during task solving. Our analysis reveals two findings. First, harness-updating is flat in base capability: models from different capability tiers produce harness updates that lead to surprisingly similar gains; even Qwen3.5-9B's updates yield gains comparable to those of Claude Opus~4.6. Second, harness-benefit is non-monotonic in base capability: weak-tier models benefit little from updated harnesses, mid-tier models benefit most, and strong-tier models benefit less than mid-tier. We trace low gains at the weak tier to two failure modes: weak-tier models may fail to activate relevant harness artifacts, or activate them but fail to follow them faithfully. These findings suggest investing capability budget in the task-solving agent rather than the evolver, and targeting harness invocation and long-horizon instruction following in agent training. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/A-EVO-Lab/a-evolve/tree/release/harness-evolution.

AI.tldr: Stronger LLMs are not necessarily better at evolving an agent’s external harness. Small and large models can produce similarly useful harness updates, but mid-tier models benefit most from those updates, while weak models often fail to use them properly.
AI.motivation: Although LLM agents are increasingly adapted through editable external harnesses instead of parameter updates, it is unclear whether stronger base task-solving models are also better at self-evolving these harnesses. The paper aims to determine which models can create useful harness updates and which models can actually exploit those updates.
AI.method: The paper studies harness self-evolution in LLM agents by separating it into two capabilities: harness-updating and harness-benefit. It evaluates models from different base-capability tiers on whether they can generate persistent harness updates from execution evidence and whether they can use updated external harness components such as prompts, skills, memories, and tools to improve task-solving.
AI.result: The study finds that harness-updating is largely flat with respect to base capability: lower-tier and higher-tier models produce updates with surprisingly similar downstream gains. It also finds that harness-benefit is non-monotonic: weak-tier models gain little, mid-tier models gain the most, and strong-tier models gain less than mid-tier models. For weak-tier models, the main failure modes are not invoking relevant harness artifacts and failing to follow them faithfully after invocation.
AI.conclusion: Harness self-evolution depends on two distinct capabilities: generating useful harness updates and benefiting from them during execution. Useful updates are produced at similar quality across model capability tiers, while the ability to benefit from those updates is strongest in mid-tier models and weaker in both weak-tier and strong-tier models.

title: Functional MRI Time Series Generation via Wavelet-Based Image Transform and Spectral Flow Matching for Brain Disorder Identification
comment: Accepted at the Fourteenth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2026)
summary: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) provides non-invasive access to dynamic brain activity by measuring blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signals over time. However, the resource-intensive nature of fMRI acquisition limits the availability of high-fidelity samples required for data-driven brain analysis models. While modern generative models can synthesize fMRI data, they often remain challenging in replicating their inherent non-stationarity, intricate spatiotemporal dynamics, and physiological variations of raw BOLD signals. To address these challenges, we propose Dual-Spectral Flow Matching (DSFM), a novel fMRI generative framework that cascades dual frequency representation of BOLD signals with spectral flow matching. Specifically, our framework first converts BOLD signals into a wavelet decomposition map via a discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to capture globalized transient and multi-scale variations, and projects into the discrete cosine transform (DCT) space across brain regions and time to exploit localized energy compaction of low-frequency dominant BOLD coefficients. Subsequently, a spectral flow matching model is trained to generate class-conditioned cosine-frequency representation. The generated samples are reconstructed through inverse DCT and inverse DWT operations to recover physiologically plausible time-domain BOLD signals. This dual-transform approach imposes structured frequency priors and preserves key physiological brain dynamics. Ultimately, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through improved downstream fMRI-based brain network classification. The code is available at https://github.com/htew0001/DSFM.git .

AI.tldr: DSFM generates better fMRI data by modeling BOLD signals in both wavelet and cosine frequency domains, then reconstructing realistic signals that help improve brain network classification.
AI.motivation: Existing fMRI generative models struggle to reproduce the non-stationarity, complex spatiotemporal structure, and physiological variability of raw BOLD signals, while real high-quality fMRI data are expensive and limited.
AI.method: The method first applies discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to BOLD signals to capture transient multi-scale variations, then projects the data into discrete cosine transform (DCT) space across regions and time to exploit low-frequency energy compaction. A class-conditioned spectral flow matching model is trained to generate the cosine-frequency representation, and inverse DCT plus inverse DWT reconstruct the final time-domain BOLD signals.
AI.result: The proposed approach generates more physiologically meaningful fMRI samples under structured frequency priors and shows improved performance on downstream fMRI-based brain network classification tasks.
AI.conclusion: DSFM is an effective generative framework for synthesizing physiologically plausible fMRI BOLD signals by combining dual spectral representations and spectral flow matching, and it improves downstream brain network classification performance.

title: Can dents and gouges compromise the structural integrity of hydrogen transport pipelines?
summary: Repurposing natural gas pipelines for hydrogen transport requires understanding how external defects, like dents and gouges, affect structural integrity under H$_2$ exposure. To address this, we combine experiments with a new hydrogen embrittlement model aimed at large plastic straining scenarios, which integrates: (i) multi-trap hydrogen transport, (ii) finite-strain plasticity, and (iii) a hydrogen- and triaxiality-dependent damage law. Each constituent of the model is validated with experiments on X65 pipeline steel: (i) hydrogen permeation, (ii) full-scale pipe-indentation, and (iii) mechanical testing at different hydrogen and triaxiality levels. The validated model is used to study \textit{passive} (indent before H$_2$ exposure) and \textit{active} (indent with H$_2$) dents and gouges. Results reveal that hydrogen does not significantly increase the damage severity of those defects, unless hydrogen egress is completely precluded at the outer surface of a pipeline that is being pressurised internally and contains a pre-existing \textit{passive} dent with a gouge.

AI.tldr: A new experimentally validated model shows that hydrogen usually does not make pipeline dents and gouges much more damaging, except in a worst-case blocked-egress passive dent-with-gouge scenario.
AI.motivation: To safely repurpose natural-gas pipelines for hydrogen transport, it is necessary to understand whether external defects such as dents and gouges become more dangerous under hydrogen exposure, especially under large plastic straining conditions that standard models may not capture well.
AI.method: The paper develops and validates a hydrogen embrittlement framework for large plastic deformation that couples multi-trap hydrogen transport, finite-strain plasticity, and a hydrogen- and triaxiality-dependent damage law. The model is calibrated and validated using hydrogen permeation tests, full-scale pipe indentation experiments, and mechanical tests under varying hydrogen content and stress triaxiality, then applied to passive and active dent/gouge scenarios.
AI.result: The validated simulations and experiments show limited hydrogen-induced amplification of defect severity for both passive and active dents/gouges. A notable exception appears when hydrogen egress at the pipe outer surface is fully blocked while the pipeline is internally pressurized and contains a passive dent with a gouge.
AI.conclusion: Hydrogen generally does not markedly worsen the structural damage caused by dents and gouges in X65 natural-gas pipelines, except in a limiting case where hydrogen cannot leave the outer surface during internal pressurization and a pre-existing passive dent with a gouge is present.

title: PithTrain: A Compact and Agent-Native MoE Training System
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has become the dominant architecture for frontier language models. To meet this demand, production frameworks have built optimized MoE training stacks over years of engineering effort. Yet evolving these stacks for new architectures and system optimizations remains expensive. With the rise of AI coding agents, they could automate parts of training-framework development and accelerate this evolution. But applying them to these existing frameworks carries hidden costs, invisible to today's throughput-only evaluations. We name this missing dimension agent-task efficiency (ATE): the cost of using coding agents to understand, operate, and extend a framework. Grounded in four agent-native design principles, we build PithTrain, a compact, agent-native MoE training framework. We further introduce ATE-Bench, covering real-world training-framework tasks. Our evaluation shows PithTrain matches the throughput of production frameworks, and on ATE-Bench, PithTrain enables higher agent-task efficiency, with up to 62% fewer Agent Turns and 64% less Active GPU Time.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that MoE frameworks should be optimized not only for training speed but also for how efficiently AI coding agents can work with them. It introduces PithTrain and ATE-Bench, showing that an agent-native design can keep throughput competitive while making framework development significantly easier for agents.
AI.motivation: Existing MoE training stacks are highly optimized for throughput but are costly to understand, operate, and extend, especially when adapting to new architectures and system optimizations. The rise of AI coding agents creates an opportunity to automate framework evolution, but current evaluations miss the hidden costs agents face when working with complex production systems.
AI.method: The paper defines agent-task efficiency (ATE) as a new evaluation dimension for coding-agent usability, proposes four agent-native design principles, builds a compact MoE training framework called PithTrain based on those principles, and introduces ATE-Bench to evaluate real-world training-framework development tasks.
AI.result: PithTrain matches the throughput of production MoE frameworks. On ATE-Bench, it improves agent-task efficiency, achieving up to 62% fewer Agent Turns and 64% less Active GPU Time.
AI.conclusion: PithTrain demonstrates that an agent-native MoE training framework can preserve production-level throughput while substantially improving agent-task efficiency, reducing both Agent Turns and Active GPU Time on realistic framework tasks.

title: Your Multimodal Speech Model Says I Have a Face for Radio
summary: As large neural models have become better at language tasks, researchers are increasingly building multi- and omnimodal models that handle more modalities of data. One example is the expansion of speech recognition models to audio-visual data for noise mitigation and multimodal subtitling. While performance and bias have been studied extensively in the single-modality regime, it is unknown how new modalities affect this, even though they produce biases in humans. We therefore propose the first bias evaluation of multimodal speech recognition, where we create videos pairing different faces with the same audio, and measure changes in speech transcription accuracy. We find large quality-of-service differences across mWhisper-Flamingo and Gemini models, with drops of up to 4.05 word error rate points, across self-declared gender, ethnicity, and their intersection. Our findings point to a priority for developers to evaluate, fix, and communicate such limitations, as providing more signals through additional modalities is not necessarily better, and may even lead to biased outcomes.

title: A Novel Global Context-aware Deep Neural Network for Enhanced Brain Tumor Segmentation using Magnetic Resonance Images
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to arXiv cs.CV
summary: Brain cancer's severity necessitates precise brain tumor segmentation, which is crucial for effective brain tumor diagnosis. Manual identification, burdened by high costs, labor, and error risks, highlights the need for automated methods. In this study, we introduce the Global Context-aware Squeeze and Excite Residual UNet (GCSER-UNet), which facilitates a fusion of spatial and channel-wise attention and thus enhances the model's capacity to capture intricate spatial dependencies and contextual information. GCSER-UNet efficiently extracts tumor segments from multimodal MRI slices, delivering exceptional performance. Evaluations on benchmark databases exhibit its superiority, achieving a notable 94 percent dice score on the TCGA LGG dataset, surpassing the state-of-the-art dice score of 91.8 percent. In the BraTS 2020 dataset, the proposed GCSER-UNet ensemble approach yielded dice scores of 95 percent, 92 percent, and 90 percent for the tumor regions - Whole Tumor (W), Tumor Core (T), and Enhancing Tumor (E), respectively. The current state-of-the-art dice scores were 94 percent, 93 percent, and 88 percent. These compelling outcomes highlight the efficacy of GCSER-UNet in precise brain tumor segmentation and thus can aid neurologists in effective brain cancer management and treatment planning.

AI.tldr: A new attention-enhanced residual U-Net, GCSER-UNet, improves brain tumor MRI segmentation by combining spatial and channel attention with global context modeling, reaching 94% Dice on TCGA LGG and strong BraTS 2020 results.
AI.motivation: Manual brain tumor segmentation is costly, labor-intensive, and error-prone, so there is a need for an automated method that can more accurately segment tumors for diagnosis and treatment planning.
AI.method: The paper proposes GCSER-UNet, a residual U-Net variant that integrates global context-aware squeeze-and-excite mechanisms with fused spatial and channel-wise attention to better model contextual and spatial dependencies for tumor segmentation.
AI.result: On TCGA LGG, the model achieved a 94% Dice score, outperforming the reported state of the art at 91.8%. On BraTS 2020, the ensemble version achieved Dice scores of 95% for Whole Tumor, 92% for Tumor Core, and 90% for Enhancing Tumor, compared with prior state-of-the-art scores of 94%, 93%, and 88%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: GCSER-UNet is an effective and competitive method for brain tumor segmentation from multimodal MRI, improving segmentation accuracy over prior approaches on major benchmarks and showing practical value for clinical support.

title: EHRBench: An Automated and Reliable EHR-based Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making with LLMs
comment: Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD 2026), Datasets and Benchmarks Track, Oral
summary: Clinical decision-making (CDM) is central to real-world clinical workflows, where clinicians infer diagnoses, select treatments, or anticipate future health outcomes under incomplete evidence. LLMs are increasingly used to support these decisions due to strong language capabilities, broad biomedical knowledge, and efficiency, yet the reliability of LLMs on real-world clinical decision tasks remains insufficiently understood. To evaluate CDM models, especially LLM-based models, an ideal and practical medical decision benchmark should be constructed via an automated yet reliable pipeline to ensure both scale and quality. Moreover, the grounding of a CDM benchmark in real patient EHRs can better support evaluation on practical CDM tasks that require substantive biomedical knowledge and clinical inference. To fill the gaps, we introduce EHRBench, an automated and reliable EHR-grounded benchmark for evaluating LLM-based clinical decision-making at scale. To ensure scalability and reliability, EHRBench is constructed through an EHR-LLM-KB(knowledge-base) interaction pipeline. For efficiency, we use a specialized LLM to automatically convert encounter-level EHR trajectories into structured templates and deterministically instantiate the templates into QA items. In parallel, we apply systematic KB-based verification and enrichment to filter hallucinated or ambiguous relations and to improve reliability. Using this pipeline, we construct nearly 1M (960,067) QA items spanning three core inference-required clinical decision tasks: diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis. We benchmark more than 30 representative LLMs on EHRBench and provide detailed analyses of performance and robustness. The results show consistent capability trends across settings, further validating the reliability of EHRBench and highlighting actionable gaps toward clinically reliable LLM systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EHRBench, a nearly 1M-item benchmark built from real EHRs via an automated LLM+knowledge-base pipeline to evaluate LLMs on diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis; tests on 30+ models show reliable benchmarking signals and clear gaps in clinical decision performance.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations do not adequately measure how reliable LLMs are on real-world clinical decision-making tasks. A practical benchmark needs both scale and quality, and grounding it in real patient EHRs better reflects diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis reasoning under incomplete evidence.
AI.method: The paper constructs EHRBench through an automated EHR-LLM-KB interaction pipeline: a specialized LLM converts encounter-level EHR trajectories into structured templates, deterministic template instantiation generates QA items, and knowledge-base verification/enrichment filters hallucinations and ambiguity while improving reliability.
AI.result: The authors build nearly 1M (960,067) QA items covering diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis, benchmark over 30 representative LLMs, and report detailed performance and robustness analyses showing stable capability trends across settings.
AI.conclusion: EHRBench provides a scalable and reliable EHR-grounded benchmark for evaluating LLM-based clinical decision-making, and the benchmarking results reveal consistent model capability trends while exposing important gaps for clinically reliable deployment.

title: A Novel Evaluation Metric for Unsupervised Learning in AIS-Based Maritime Anomaly Detection: MADQI
comment: 26 pages, A new Eval Metric for Unsupervised Machine Learning
summary: This paper introduces a new systematic framework for detecting anomalies in maritime Automatic Identification System (AIS) datasets. These anomalies include abnormal vessel behaviours related to speed, position jumps, time gaps, and turn angles. Although unsupervised learning algorithms such as Isolation Forest are widely used for detecting anomalous vessel movements, they often lack systematic and meaningful evaluation measures. To address this limitation, we propose a novel quality metric called Maritime Anomaly Detection Quality Index (MADQI). The prosed MADQI is a composite index designed to evaluate the anomaly detection performance of machine learning models without requiring labelled data. The proposed framework uses Haversine distance calculations to analyse AIS datasets and identify anomalies based on their spatial and behavioural characteristics. The proposed MADQI evaluation framework integrates four interconnected metrics: Anomaly Rate Consistency (ARC), Physical Plausibility Score (PPS), Score Distribution Separation (SDS), and Extreme Case Evidence (ECE). These metrics are combined through automatic normalisation using multi-chunk evaluation and adaptive scaling techniques. Experimental results on the AIS dataset show that the proposed framework achieved a MADQI score of 80.37%, demonstrating its effectiveness for unsupervised anomaly detection. In particular, the algorithm performed strongly in identifying abnormal vessel behaviour. Among the individual MADQI components, ECE and ARC achieved scores of 0.907 and 1.000, respectively, indicating excellent capability in detecting extreme anomalies and maintaining anomaly rate consistency. Overall, these results are encouraging and demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a reliable and meaningful approach for evaluating unsupervised anomaly detection in maritime AIS data.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MADQI, a new label-free metric framework to evaluate unsupervised maritime AIS anomaly detection. Using spatial-behavioral analysis and four combined quality metrics, it achieves an 80.37% overall score and shows strong effectiveness for evaluating abnormal vessel movement detection.
AI.motivation: The motivation is that existing unsupervised anomaly detection approaches for maritime AIS data, such as Isolation Forest, are widely used but lack systematic, meaningful, and label-free evaluation measures for judging model quality.
AI.method: The method builds a systematic AIS anomaly detection and evaluation framework using Haversine-distance-based analysis of vessel trajectories to detect anomalies in speed, position jumps, time gaps, and turn angles. It introduces MADQI, a composite unlabeled evaluation index combining four metrics: ARC, PPS, SDS, and ECE, with automatic normalization via multi-chunk evaluation and adaptive scaling.
AI.result: Experiments on AIS data produced a MADQI score of 80.37%. The framework performed strongly in identifying abnormal vessel behaviour, with ECE scoring 0.907 and ARC scoring 1.000, indicating excellent detection of extreme anomalies and stable anomaly rate consistency.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that its MADQI-based framework offers a reliable and meaningful way to evaluate unsupervised anomaly detection in maritime AIS data without labelled data, achieving a MADQI score of 80.37% and showing strong performance especially in extreme anomaly detection and anomaly rate consistency.

title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Uncertainty Quantification Methodologies for Predicting Turbine Gas Temperature Degradation
summary: Effective prognostics and health management of modern engines relies on accurate turbine gas temperature predictions and robust uncertainty quantification to ensure reliability and safety. This paper investigates five major approaches for constructing prediction intervals -- namely the Delta method, Bayesian Monte Carlo Dropout, Bootstrap method, Lower-Upper Bound Estimation, and Mean-Variance Estimation -- as a means of capturing the uncertainty in neural network predictions of turbine gas temperature. Each approach is implemented within a unified experimental framework that employs cross-validation for hyperparameter selection, repeated train-test splits for performance robustness, and multiple metrics to evaluate both the accuracy and tightness of the intervals. In particular, Coverage Probability, Normalized Mean Prediction Interval Width, and the Coverage Width-based Criterion are measured to comprehensively assess each method's reliability and sharpness. Experiments conducted on a representative turbine gas temperature dataset reveal distinct trade-offs among the five methods in terms of interval coverage, width, and stability. These findings provide a practical guide for selecting and tuning prediction interval methods in engine health management and prognostics, ensuring both interpretability and precision in real-world applications.

AI.tldr: This paper compares five neural-network prediction interval methods for turbine gas temperature forecasting and finds that each method has different trade-offs between interval coverage, width, and stability, providing a practical reference for uncertainty-aware engine health management.
AI.motivation: The motivation is that modern engine prognostics and health management requires accurate turbine gas temperature prediction together with robust uncertainty quantification to support reliability, safety, interpretability, and practical deployment.
AI.method: The study implements five prediction interval construction approaches within a unified neural-network-based experimental framework: the Delta method, Bayesian Monte Carlo Dropout, Bootstrap, Lower-Upper Bound Estimation, and Mean-Variance Estimation. It uses cross-validation for hyperparameter tuning, repeated train-test splits for robustness, and evaluates the methods with Coverage Probability, Normalized Mean Prediction Interval Width, and Coverage Width-based Criterion.
AI.result: Experiments on a representative turbine gas temperature dataset show clear differences among the five methods in terms of reliability, sharpness, and stability of prediction intervals. The comparative evaluation highlights the practical strengths and weaknesses of each method under a common framework.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that no single prediction interval method is universally best for turbine gas temperature prediction. Instead, the five methods show different trade-offs in coverage, interval width, and stability, and the results offer practical guidance for selecting and tuning uncertainty quantification methods in engine prognostics and health management.

title: When English Rewrites Local Knowledge: Global Narrative Dominance in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as cross-lingual knowledge interfaces. However, culturally grounded questions often reflect globally dominant narratives rather than local contexts. We study this failure mode as \textit{global narrative dominance} in Bangla, a low-resource cultural context. We introduce \texttt{CulturalNB}, a dataset of 717 manually curated Bengali cultural instances with parallel Bangla--English question--answer pairs and supporting evidence, metadata, and sociocultural annotations. Using question-only and evidence-based prompting, we evaluate nine state-of-the-art LLMs with human and two independent LLM judges across metrics for cross-lingual consistency, language anchoring, global substitution, institutional bias, and epistemic perspective coverage. Results show that questions asked in English systematically increase global substitution and institutional framing while reducing local perspective coverage. Local evidence improves factual consistency and perspective coverage, but does not eliminate language-induced epistemic shifts. These findings suggest that cultural failures in LLMs are not only missing-knowledge errors but also failures of grounding and narrative prioritization.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that multilingual LLMs answering Bengali cultural questions tend to privilege global narratives, especially when the question is asked in English. A new benchmark, CulturalNB, reveals that local evidence helps but does not fully fix these culturally grounded reasoning failures.
AI.motivation: LLMs are commonly used as cross-lingual knowledge interfaces, but culturally grounded questions are often answered through globally dominant narratives instead of local cultural context, especially in low-resource settings such as Bangla.
AI.method: The paper introduces CulturalNB, a manually curated dataset of 717 Bengali cultural instances with parallel Bangla-English QA pairs, evidence, metadata, and sociocultural annotations. It evaluates nine state-of-the-art LLMs under question-only and evidence-based prompting, using human judges and two independent LLM judges across metrics including cross-lingual consistency, language anchoring, global substitution, institutional bias, and epistemic perspective coverage.
AI.result: English prompts systematically worsen cultural grounding by increasing global substitution and institutional bias while decreasing local perspective coverage. Supplying local evidence improves factual consistency and perspective coverage, but residual epistemic differences remain across languages.
AI.conclusion: LLMs exhibit global narrative dominance in Bangla cultural QA: asking in English increases global substitution and institutional framing, while reducing local perspective coverage. Evidence helps but does not fully remove language-induced epistemic shifts.

title: OmniMem: Scalable and Adaptive Memory Retrieval for Long Video Generation
summary: Autoregressive (AR) video generation extends videos by producing latent chunks sequentially, but scaling to long videos requires repeated access to a growing historical KV cache. Existing methods reduce this cost by truncating the KV cache or compressing it into implicit memory, but both lose explicit access to query-relevant historical details. We propose OmniMem, an explicit full-range memory retrieval framework that performs sparse KV retrieval over the historical cache. To make this practical for chunk-based AR video generation, OmniMem addresses two issues: (i) local bias in sparse KV selection and (ii) Union Explosion in memory access. Adaptive Window Exclusion removes local-window blocks from the selection candidates when sufficient long-range history is available, preserving the sparse budget for informative long-range retrieval. Query-Shared KV Selection reduces cross-query diversity, while Per-Head Scattered KV Access avoids expanding head-specific selections into a large selected KV buffer. This allows each attention head to retrieve non-contiguous KV blocks according to its own selection pattern. Experiments on long-video generation show that OmniMem improves Dynamic Degree by 52.3% and preserves strong consistency over strong baselines, while maintaining comparable memory usage.

AI.tldr: OmniMem lets autoregressive video models explicitly retrieve sparse, relevant KV blocks from the entire history, fixing local-bias and memory-access inefficiencies to generate longer, more dynamic, and consistent videos.
AI.motivation: Existing long-video AR generation methods either truncate the KV cache or compress it into implicit memory, which reduces cost but loses explicit access to query-relevant historical details needed for long-range coherence.
AI.method: The paper proposes sparse KV retrieval over the full historical cache and introduces Adaptive Window Exclusion to counter local selection bias, Query-Shared KV Selection to reduce cross-query diversity, and Per-Head Scattered KV Access to avoid union explosion during head-specific memory access.
AI.result: On long-video generation benchmarks, OmniMem improves Dynamic Degree by 52.3%, preserves strong consistency compared with strong baselines, and maintains comparable memory usage.
AI.conclusion: OmniMem is an explicit full-range memory retrieval framework for chunk-based autoregressive video generation that improves long-video dynamics and consistency while keeping memory usage comparable to strong baselines.

title: Structure-Induced Information for Rerooting Levin Tree Search
summary: Subgoal-based policy tree search, which uses a policy to guide search, is effective for complex single-agent deterministic problems but often relies on explicit subgoal generation that can incur substantial overhead and hinders scalability. In this paper, we overcome these limitations by using a learned ``rerooter'' through the recently-introduced $\sqrt{\text{LTS}}$ algorithm. A rerooter implicitly decomposes the problem into soft subtasks. While previous work focused on the formal guarantees for given or handcrafted rerooters, in this work we propose three rerooter designs: (i) a clustering-based rerooter that exploits global state-space structure, (ii) a heuristic-based rerooter that leverages learned cost-to-go estimates, and (iii) a hybrid that combines both signals. Our framework avoids having to explicitly reconstruct and reason over generated subgoals, thereby enabling scalable allocation of search effort with significantly lower computational overhead. Empirically, our rerooting-based methods scale to complex environments where subgoal-based policy tree search fails, and achieve state-of-the-art online training efficiency on the domains tested.

AI.tldr: The paper replaces expensive explicit subgoal generation in policy tree search with learned rerooters in sqrt(LTS), proposing clustering, heuristic, and hybrid rerooters that scale better and train more efficiently.
AI.motivation: Existing subgoal-based policy tree search works well on complex deterministic single-agent problems but depends on explicit subgoal generation, which introduces substantial computational overhead and limits scalability.
AI.method: The paper proposes three rerooter designs for sqrt(LTS): a clustering-based rerooter using global state-space structure, a heuristic-based rerooter using learned cost-to-go estimates, and a hybrid combining both signals.
