AI.result: Empirically, the rerooting-based methods scale to complex environments where traditional subgoal-based policy tree search fails, and they achieve state-of-the-art online training efficiency on the tested domains.
AI.conclusion: Using learned rerooters within the sqrt(LTS) framework can replace explicit subgoal generation, reducing overhead and improving scalability while achieving strong empirical performance.

title: NumLeak: Public Numeric Benchmarks as Latent Labels in Foundation Models
comment: 23 pages, 12 figures, 17 tables. Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on the Impact of Memorization on Trustworthy Foundation Models (MemFM)
summary: Public numeric benchmarks appear in pretraining, so an evaluation that conditions on a date may be measuring memorized recall rather than out-of-sample skill. We introduce NumLeak, a measurement framework that combines API-boundary probes on production models with a white-box controlled validation on an open causal LM. Top-tier frontier LLMs recall the Fama-French market excess return at 3-seed pooled Pearson r=0.97-0.99 while staying within 0.15 within-25bps on the five sibling factors; comparable fidelity appears on U.S. unemployment, CPI inflation, and NOAA temperature. On a recent-release holdout, parse rate collapses to 21-57% but r stays at approximately 0.99 on months answered, the refuse-or-recall asymmetry a memorized channel predicts. The white-box experiment reproduces the dose-response, and logprob ranking detects memorization that open-ended generation misses, implying closed-API black-box probes understate the channel. A Sonnet "date to market-sentiment" regression that correlates with true Mkt-RF at r=0.74 collapses to r=0.02 once the model's own recall is residualized out. A one-line system-prompt defense blocks 99.8% of a non-adaptive single-turn suffix attack set at near-zero utility cost on conceptual and historical-narrative queries

AI.tldr: LLMs can memorize and regurgitate public numeric time series from pretraining, making date-conditioned benchmark results look like skill when they may just be recall. NumLeak measures this with black-box and white-box tests, shows near-perfect recall on several datasets, and finds that simple prompt defenses can largely shut down an attack path.
AI.motivation: Many public numeric benchmarks are present in pretraining corpora, so strong benchmark performance may reflect memorized retrieval rather than genuine generalization or forecasting skill. The work aims to measure this leakage channel directly and quantify its implications for evaluation and downstream claims.
AI.method: The paper introduces NumLeak, a framework combining black-box API probes on production LLMs with white-box controlled validation on an open causal language model. It tests recall of time-indexed public numeric series, measures correlation and accuracy on answered months, evaluates recent-release holdouts, uses log-probability ranking to detect latent memorization, analyzes a downstream market-sentiment regression, and studies a one-line system-prompt defense against suffix attacks.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs nearly perfectly recall several public macro/finance/weather series such as Fama-French Mkt-RF, unemployment, CPI inflation, and NOAA temperature, with pooled Pearson correlations around 0.97-0.99. On recent-release holdouts, answer rates drop sharply but correlations remain about 0.99 on answered cases, supporting a refuse-or-recall memorization pattern. White-box experiments reproduce a dose-response relationship, logprob ranking reveals additional hidden memorization, residualizing model recall removes most of an apparent market-sentiment signal, and a simple system prompt blocks 99.8% of a non-adaptive attack set at near-zero utility cost.
AI.conclusion: Public numeric benchmarks can leak through pretraining into LLM recall, so date-conditioned evaluations may overestimate true out-of-sample reasoning ability. Black-box probing likely understates this memorization channel, but simple prompt-level defenses can sharply reduce exploitability with little utility loss.

title: Scientific Machine Learning for Engine Health Management and Remaining Useful Life Prediction
summary: Engine Health Management (EHM) depends on reliable forecasting of Remaining Useful Life (RUL) and on tracking thermal indicators such as turbine gas temperature (TGT). In practice, real-world fleet data are heterogeneous and non-stationary, and point predictions alone are insufficient for risk-aware maintenance decisions. This paper presents a multi-task scientific machine learning framework for turbine prognostics that jointly predicts turbine gas temperature untrimmed (TGTU), Delta Turbine Gas Temperature (DTGT), and RUL, with quantified uncertainty in the form of prediction intervals whose empirical coverage is evaluated. A shared sequence encoder (convolutional front-end with residual bidirectional LSTM layers and attention pooling) feeds task-specific heads, including mean--variance estimation for probabilistic regression and, optionally, a survival head for threshold-based event modeling. The framework is designed to be tunable via a small set of practitioner-facing parameters (e.g., DTGT thresholding rules and RUL target construction) so that deployment can align with in-house policies and proprietary criteria. The predictive performance of the proposed framework is evaluated using both point and interval metrics, including mean absolute error (MAE), prediction interval coverage probability (PICP), mean prediction interval width (MPIW), and the coverage--width criterion (CWC). Results are reported both in aggregate and stratified by flight phase and maintenance segment to highlight operational-context effects and to support uncertainty-aware monitoring.

AI.tldr: A tunable multi-task deep learning framework jointly predicts turbine thermal indicators and engine RUL, while also estimating prediction intervals so maintenance teams can make risk-aware decisions under real-world fleet variability.
AI.motivation: The motivation is that engine health management requires reliable Remaining Useful Life prediction and thermal tracking, but real fleet data are heterogeneous and non-stationary. Point predictions alone are not sufficient for risk-aware maintenance, so a framework is needed that jointly models multiple prognostic targets and quantifies predictive uncertainty.
AI.method: The method uses a shared sequence encoder composed of a convolutional front-end, residual bidirectional LSTM layers, and attention pooling, followed by task-specific heads for TGTU, DTGT, and RUL. It employs probabilistic mean-variance regression for uncertainty estimation and can optionally include a survival-analysis head for threshold-based event modeling. The framework is configurable through practitioner-facing parameters such as DTGT threshold rules and RUL target definitions.
AI.result: The reported results show the framework is evaluated with both point and interval metrics, including MAE, PICP, MPIW, and CWC, with performance presented in aggregate and also stratified by flight phase and maintenance segment to expose operational-context effects. The abstract indicates the framework supports uncertainty-aware monitoring, though it does not provide specific numerical outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that a multi-task scientific machine learning framework can jointly forecast TGTU, DTGT, and RUL while providing calibrated prediction intervals, and that evaluating results by operational context such as flight phase and maintenance segment improves uncertainty-aware engine health monitoring and maintenance decision support.

title: Configurable Reward Model for Balanced Safety Alignment
summary: Aligning large language models (LLMs) to heterogeneous and rapidly evolving safety requirements remains a critical challenge. Existing instruction-tuned LLMs and standalone safety classifiers often fail to generalize to new safety configurations, motivating the need for Reward Models (RMs) that are explicitly configurable to changing specifications. We introduce the Configurable Safety Reward Model (CSRM), which is jointly optimized for calibrated safety compliance and reward modeling. Our approach is supported by configuration-targeted data augmentation that enforces instruction adherence while preserving relative severity structure. The resulting RM is sensitive to fine-grained safety configurations and conversational nuances, substantially improving generalization to previously unseen safety configurations. CSRM achieves state-of-the-art performance on recent configurable safety benchmarks, including CoSApien (94.6% F1) and DynaBench (75.8% F1), without requiring additional human annotation. When used for downstream safety alignment, CSRM yields LLMs with a significantly improved helpfulness-safety tradeoff compared to existing baselines.

AI.tldr: A new configurable safety reward model lets LLM safety behavior adapt to changing rules, generalizes better to unseen configurations, and sets new benchmark results without extra annotation.
AI.motivation: Existing instruction-tuned LLMs and standalone safety classifiers do not generalize well to heterogeneous, evolving safety specifications, so a configurable reward model is needed.
AI.method: The paper proposes a Configurable Safety Reward Model jointly trained for calibrated safety compliance and reward modeling, supported by configuration-targeted data augmentation that preserves relative severity while enforcing instruction adherence.
AI.result: CSRM reaches state-of-the-art results on configurable safety benchmarks, including 94.6% F1 on CoSApien and 75.8% F1 on DynaBench, and improves the helpfulness-safety tradeoff in downstream aligned LLMs.
AI.conclusion: CSRM can flexibly adapt to changing safety requirements and improves both configurable safety evaluation and downstream LLM alignment, achieving strong generalization without extra human annotation.

title: Healthcare Mechanisms from Policy-as-Code Search under Strategic Provider Response
summary: Healthcare mechanisms are inseparable from the strategic provider response they induce: existing healthcare AI benchmarks hold this response fixed and so cannot evaluate mechanisms by the equilibrium they produce. We recast hospital mechanism design as program synthesis for language models: typed, inspectable rule programs are executed and scored by Medi-Sim, a multi-agent simulator with five strategic provider channels (coding, selection, delay, effort, triage). An incentive sweep recovers classical health-economics findings as adjacent regimes -- up-coding and low-complexity-patient selection under profit pressure, and Goodhart-style drift where measured performance becomes anti-correlated with true outcomes -- and a single audit lever exposes pressure migration: closing the coding channel more than doubles low-complexity selection. LLM-guided evolutionary code search over the same rule-program space then synthesizes an inspectable mixed-objective program that eliminates up-coding, halves rejection, and retains most of the profit-oriented baseline's funds.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a simulator-based framework for designing hospital incentive mechanisms under strategic provider behavior, then uses LLM-guided search to find an interpretable mechanism that reduces gaming and patient rejection while preserving much of the money flow.
AI.motivation: Existing healthcare AI benchmarks hold provider behavior fixed, so they fail to evaluate healthcare mechanisms under strategic adaptation. The motivation is to design and assess mechanisms based on the equilibrium behaviors they generate when providers respond strategically across multiple channels.
AI.method: The method recasts hospital mechanism design as program synthesis for language models. Typed, inspectable rule programs are executed inside Medi-Sim, a multi-agent simulator modeling five strategic provider response channels: coding, selection, delay, effort, and triage. The authors run incentive sweeps to study induced equilibria, then apply LLM-guided evolutionary code search over the same program space to synthesize improved mechanisms.
AI.result: The incentive sweep reproduces classical health-economics phenomena in nearby regimes, including up-coding, selection of low-complexity patients under profit pressure, and Goodhart-style drift where measured performance becomes anti-correlated with true outcomes. The study also finds pressure migration: restricting coding more than doubles low-complexity selection. The synthesized mixed-objective rule program eliminates up-coding, halves rejection, and keeps most of the profit-oriented baseline’s funds.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that healthcare payment/mechanism design must be evaluated by the strategic equilibria they induce, not by fixed-behavior benchmarks. By framing mechanism design as synthesizing typed rule programs and evaluating them in a multi-agent simulator, the authors can both recover known adverse-incentive regimes and automatically discover a mixed-objective mechanism that reduces gaming while preserving much of the financial objective.

title: LongDS-Bench: On the Failure of Long-Horizon Agentic Data Analysis
summary: Real-world data analysis is inherently iterative, yet existing benchmarks mostly evaluate isolated or short interactive tasks, leaving agents' ability to track evolving analytical context over long horizons untested. We introduce LongDS, a benchmark for long-horizon, multi-turn data analysis where agents must maintain, update, restore, and compose evolving analytical states. LongDS comprises 68 tasks constructed from real-world Kaggle notebooks, spanning 2,225 turns across six domains including Geoscience, Business, and Education. Tasks are designed around state-evolution patterns (e.g., counterfactual perturbation, rollback, multi-state composition), with an average dependency span of 11.3 turns. Evaluating five state-of-the-art models, we find that the best model reaches only 48.45% average accuracy, performance drops nearly 47 points from early to late turns, and long-horizon errors account for 52%--69% of failures. Further analysis shows that additional agent steps do not necessarily improve performance, suggesting that the key bottleneck is maintaining a correct analytical state rather than increasing interaction budget. We release LongDS to support research on reliable long-horizon agentic data analysis. Code and data will be released at https://github.com/zjunlp/DataMind.

AI.tldr: LongDS is a new benchmark for multi-turn, long-horizon data analysis. Tests on five strong models show that current agents often fail because they cannot reliably maintain analytical state over time, not because they lack enough interaction steps.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks mainly test isolated or short interactive data-analysis tasks, which fails to measure whether agents can preserve and update analytical context over long iterative workflows that reflect real-world data analysis.
AI.method: The paper introduces LongDS, a benchmark built from 68 real-world Kaggle notebook-based tasks covering 2,225 turns across six domains. The tasks are structured around analytical state-evolution patterns such as counterfactual perturbation, rollback, and multi-state composition, and five state-of-the-art models are evaluated on these long-horizon multi-turn tasks.
AI.result: The best evaluated model achieves only 48.45% average accuracy. Performance declines by nearly 47 percentage points from early to late turns, and 52% to 69% of failures are caused by long-horizon errors. Additional agent steps do not consistently improve outcomes.
AI.conclusion: LongDS reveals that current state-of-the-art agents are weak at long-horizon data analysis because they struggle to correctly maintain and compose evolving analytical states over many turns; improving state tracking is more important than simply allowing more interaction steps.

title: CanLegalRAGBench: Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Canadian Case Law
summary: RAG-based legal assistants have been growing in popularity, but LLM hallucinations remain a key issue and potentially undermines justice. While benchmarks have been developed to evaluate progress, many rely on synthetic queries rather than realistic legal scenarios. Moreover, Canadian law remains underrepresented in existing evaluations. To address this gap, we introduce CanLegalRAGBench, a Canadian legal QA benchmark based on realistic queries and expert-annotated answers grounded in case law. Our evaluation shows that retrieval performance is sensitive to design choices and that open-source embedding models are competitive with closed source models. However, it also reveals the limitation of automatic evaluations that penalize systems for retrieving alternative relevant documents. We also find that generated answers often diverge from gold responses, either with hallucinations or by producing overly detailed or irrelevant content, with 8-29% of claims not being supported by the retrieved documents. We hope this benchmark will help drive continued progress in addressing limitations of legal RAG systems.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a realistic Canadian legal RAG benchmark and shows that while some retrieval setups work well, legal RAG systems still suffer from evaluation flaws and significant hallucination/faithfulness problems.
AI.motivation: Existing legal RAG benchmarks often use synthetic queries and insufficiently cover Canadian law, which limits realistic evaluation of hallucination risks in legal assistants.
AI.method: The paper introduces a Canadian legal QA benchmark built from realistic legal queries and expert-annotated answers grounded in case law, then evaluates RAG systems under different retrieval design choices, embedding models, and automatic/manual assessment perspectives.
AI.result: Retrieval quality is highly sensitive to system design; open-source embedding models can match closed-source alternatives; automatic evaluation can unfairly penalize retrieval of alternative relevant documents; generated answers frequently diverge from gold answers, with 8-29% of claims unsupported by retrieved documents.
AI.conclusion: CanLegalRAGBench fills an important gap for evaluating legal RAG in Canadian law using realistic, expert-annotated QA, and the benchmark highlights persistent weaknesses in retrieval and answer faithfulness.

title: Seeing Isn't Knowing: Do VLMs Know When Not to Answer Spatial Questions (and Why)?
summary: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental capability for vision-language models (VLMs) deployed in real-world environments. However, visual observations are inherently limited representations of a 3D world: occlusion can render objects invisible, and perspective can make geometric properties misleading. Despite this, existing spatial reasoning benchmarks typically assume that observations are sufficient and reliable, focusing on whether models produce correct answers rather than whether they recognize when a question cannot be answered and what additional observations would be needed. In this work, we challenge this assumption by constructing a controlled evaluation framework, SpatialUncertain, and introducing two types of observation challenges: (1) occlusion, which hides target information, and (2) perspective ambiguity, which produces misleading visual cues. For each configuration, we design spatial questions that are answerable under clean observations but require abstention under the introduced challenges. We further evaluate whether models can identify which additional viewpoints would resolve perspective ambiguity. Our results across a diverse set of frontier open- and closed-source VLMs reveal two consistent failure modes. First, models are prone to overconfident answering, attempting to solve spatial reasoning tasks even when visual evidence is incomplete or misleading, with average accuracy around 30\% under occlusion and below 10\% under perspective ambiguity. Second, even when additional views are available, some models perform near random chance in identifying which would provide reliable evidence. Together, our findings call for moving beyond answer correctness toward evaluating whether models know when to abstain and how to seek reliable evidence.

AI.tldr: SpatialUncertain shows that state-of-the-art VLMs are poor at handling uncertain spatial evidence: they should often abstain but instead guess, and they also struggle to decide which extra views would resolve ambiguity.
AI.motivation: Existing spatial reasoning benchmarks for vision-language models generally assume visual observations are sufficient and reliable. This ignores real-world 3D limitations such as occlusion and perspective distortion, and fails to assess whether models know when a question is unanswerable or what extra evidence is required.
AI.method: The paper introduces SpatialUncertain, a controlled evaluation framework for spatial reasoning under uncertainty. It creates two observation challenges: occlusion, which hides target information, and perspective ambiguity, which creates misleading geometric cues. For each setup, the authors design questions that are answerable with clean observations but should trigger abstention under the challenged observations, and they also test whether models can choose extra viewpoints that would resolve ambiguity.
AI.result: Across a range of open- and closed-source frontier VLMs, the authors find two major failure modes: severe overconfident answering under incomplete or misleading observations, with average accuracy around 30% under occlusion and below 10% under perspective ambiguity; and weak ability to identify informative additional viewpoints, with some models performing near random chance.
AI.conclusion: Current vision-language models lack calibrated spatial uncertainty handling: they often answer confidently when observations are insufficient or misleading, and they struggle to identify what additional viewpoints are needed. Evaluation should therefore go beyond answer correctness to include abstention and evidence-seeking.

title: MAVEN: Improving Generalization in Agentic Tool Calling
summary: Generalization across agentic tool-calling environments remains a central challenge for reliable agentic reasoning systems. Although large language models achieve strong results on individual benchmarks, their ability to compose reasoning strategies, preserve intermediate states, and coordinate tools across domains remains underexplored. We present MAVEN (Modular Agentic Verification and Execution Network), a lightweight symbolic reasoning scaffold for structured decomposition, adaptive tool orchestration, and intermediate verification. We evaluate MAVEN across established tool-calling benchmarks, including BFCL v3, TauBench, Tau2Bench, AceBench, and introduce MAVEN-Bench, a stress-test benchmark for multi-step mathematical and physical reasoning with explicit verification and adversarial task composition. MAVEN-Bench exposes a substantial gap between partial reasoning quality and end-to-end task success; in direct MAVEN-Bench runs, MAVEN improves its GPT-OSS-120b base model from 48% to 71% accuracy without additional training. It also remains competitive with frontier proprietary baselines while using an open-weight backbone with an estimated cost ratio of roughly 1/10, suggesting that lightweight verification-centered scaffolds can strengthen compositional reasoning and motivate more process-aware evaluation of agents in the wild.

AI.tldr: MAVEN adds modular decomposition plus step-by-step verification to an open-weight LLM, boosting hard multi-step tool-use reasoning from 48% to 71% on a new benchmark without retraining, while staying much cheaper than proprietary alternatives.
AI.motivation: Current large language models perform well on isolated agentic benchmarks, but their cross-environment generalization, ability to preserve intermediate states, compose reasoning strategies, and reliably coordinate tools across domains are still insufficiently understood and limited.
AI.method: The paper proposes MAVEN, a modular agentic scaffold that performs structured task decomposition, adaptive tool orchestration, and intermediate verification on top of a base large language model. It is evaluated on multiple existing tool-calling benchmarks and a newly introduced stress-test benchmark, MAVEN-Bench.
AI.result: Across BFCL v3, TauBench, Tau2Bench, AceBench, and the new MAVEN-Bench, MAVEN is competitive with strong proprietary baselines. On direct MAVEN-Bench runs, it improves the GPT-OSS-120b base model from 48% to 71% accuracy without extra training, and does so at an estimated cost of about one-tenth of frontier proprietary systems.
AI.conclusion: MAVEN demonstrates that a lightweight, verification-centered symbolic reasoning scaffold can substantially improve compositional tool-using reasoning across domains without additional training, while remaining cost-efficient relative to proprietary frontier systems.

title: Calibrated Preference Learning: The Case of Label Ranking
summary: Calibration, the alignment of predicted probabilities with true outcome frequencies, is essential for reliable decision-making. While extensively studied for classification and regression, calibration has not been formally addressed for probabilistic label ranking, where the goal is to predict a distribution over orderings of a label set. Naively treating rankings as classes ignores their structure and fails to capture important modalities such as pairwise and top-k predictions. We formalize calibration for label ranking and develop a hierarchy of notions covering full rankings, sub-rankings, and top-k rankings. We prove that full-rank calibration implies the others but not conversely, and sub-ranking and top-k calibration are incomparable. Empirically, we find popular label ranking models are often poorly calibrated, with substantial differences between sub-ranking and top-k metrics. Applying our framework to RLHF reward models, we find that calibration correlates strongly but not perfectly with benchmark accuracy, suggesting it captures a meaningful quality dimension beyond top-1 accuracy. These findings motivate future work on understanding the downstream effects of miscalibration and developing methods to correct it.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first formal framework for calibration in probabilistic label ranking, defines full-rank, sub-ranking, and top-k calibration, proves how they relate, and shows through experiments that common models are often miscalibrated. In RLHF, calibration provides an extra quality signal beyond simple accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing calibration research focuses on classification and regression, but not on probabilistic label ranking, where predictions are distributions over label orderings. Treating rankings as flat classes loses structural information and misses practically important views such as pairwise, sub-ranking, and top-k behavior. The paper is motivated by the need for reliable uncertainty estimation in this richer prediction setting.
AI.method: The authors formalize calibration for probabilistic label ranking by defining calibration notions for full rankings, sub-rankings, and top-k rankings. They theoretically analyze implication and incomparability relations among these notions, and empirically evaluate popular label ranking models and RLHF reward models under the proposed calibration metrics.
AI.result: The paper proves that full-rank calibration implies sub-ranking and top-k calibration, while the reverse does not hold; sub-ranking and top-k calibration are also incomparable. Experiments show that widely used label ranking models are often poorly calibrated and can differ substantially across calibration metrics. In RLHF reward models, calibration is strongly correlated with, but not identical to, benchmark accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that calibration for probabilistic label ranking needs its own formal treatment. It establishes a hierarchy of calibration notions, shows clear logical relations and separations among them, and demonstrates empirically that existing models are often miscalibrated. It also finds that calibration captures model quality beyond top-1 accuracy in RLHF reward models.

title: Linear Ensembles Wash Away Watermarks: On the Fragility of Distributional Perturbations in LLMs
summary: Watermarking embeds statistical signatures in AI-generated text for detection and attribution. We reveal a fundamental vulnerability: when users access multiple models (today's reality), watermarks trivially fail. Watermarks perturb output distributions away from the original, and in competitive markets, these perturbations are typically independent across providers. We theoretically prove that averaging output probability distributions recovers the unwatermarked distribution with up to a second-order error term. Empirically, simply averaging 3-5 models cancels out these perturbations. We introduce WASH (Watermark Attenuation via Statistical Hybridisation), which solves practical challenges in ensemble generation: vocabulary misalignment and tokenisation differences across heterogeneous models. Experiments across six watermarking schemes and three LLMs show that averaging across 3 models suppresses detection z-scores from 5-300 to below 2 (below the detection threshold of 4) and reduces TPR at 5% FPR to below 50%, while improving quality by 27.5% and running 6 times faster than the best baseline on the long sequence generation. Our results suggest that robust AI-text detection via watermarking requires either accepting this fundamental vulnerability or unprecedented coordination among model providers.

AI.tldr: Multi-model averaging can break current AI text watermarks. The paper proves why this happens, introduces WASH to make cross-model averaging practical, and shows that using only a few models can defeat detection while improving quality and speed.
AI.motivation: The motivation is that existing watermarking work often assumes access to only one model, while real users increasingly have access to multiple competing models. Since watermarking changes model output distributions and these changes are typically independent across providers, the authors investigate whether multi-model use creates a fundamental weakness for watermark-based detection and attribution.
AI.method: The authors provide a theoretical analysis showing that averaging output probability distributions from multiple watermarked models cancels watermark perturbations up to a second-order error term. They then propose WASH (Watermark Attenuation via Statistical Hybridisation) to enable practical ensemble generation across heterogeneous models by handling vocabulary and tokenization mismatches, and evaluate it across six watermarking schemes and three LLMs.
AI.result: Empirically, averaging only 3 to 5 models substantially suppresses watermark signals. Across six watermarking schemes and three LLMs, combining three models reduces detection z-scores from 5-300 to below 2, lowers TPR at 5% FPR to below 50%, improves generation quality by 27.5%, and is 6 times faster than the best baseline for long-sequence generation.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that text watermarking for AI-generated content is fundamentally fragile in realistic multi-provider settings. By averaging outputs from several independently watermarked models, users can largely recover the original unwatermarked distribution, making current watermark detectors unreliable unless providers coordinate unusually closely.

title: VLM3: Vision Language Models Are Native 3D Learners
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) enable a unified model to solve various vision tasks through prompting. They have shown promising performance in semantic understanding. However, 3D understanding still largely relies on expert vision models with complex task-specific designs. The key argument this work wants to make is that VLMs are native 3D learners. Our in-depth large scale study shows that 1) focal length unification, 2) text-based pixel reference and 3) data mixture and scaling, are all you need for effective 3D learning. Model architecture changes, large models, heavy data augmentations, and complex losses including the regression formulation, many of which form the foundation of expert vision models, are actually not necessary conditions. As a result, we propose VLM3, a scalable method with the simplest design that enables standard VLMs to master diverse 3D tasks. VLM3 not only advances the VLM depth estimation accuracy by a large margin (0.84 -> 0.9), but also enables diverse 3D tasks such as pixel correspondence, camera pose estimation and object-level 3D understanding, matching expert vision model accuracy while maintaining standard architectures and text-based training. We believe VLM3 opens up a new paradigm for simple and scalable 3D learning.

AI.tldr: VLM3 argues that vision-language models are naturally capable of 3D learning: with focal length unification, text-based pixel references, and large mixed data, standard VLMs can solve diverse 3D tasks without specialized 3D model designs.
AI.motivation: Although VLMs perform well on semantic vision tasks, 3D understanding still depends heavily on specialized expert models with complicated task-specific designs. The paper is motivated by testing whether these complexities are truly necessary, and whether VLMs can natively learn 3D perception in a simpler unified framework.
AI.method: The paper conducts a large-scale empirical study and proposes VLM3, a simple training paradigm for 3D learning with standard VLM architectures. The approach relies on three main ingredients: unified focal length handling, text-based pixel referencing, and mixed/scaled training data, while avoiding specialized architectures, heavy augmentations, and complex regression-style losses.
AI.result: VLM3 significantly improves VLM-based depth estimation accuracy from 0.84 to 0.90 and extends capability to multiple 3D tasks including pixel correspondence, camera pose estimation, and object-level 3D understanding. It achieves performance comparable to expert vision models while preserving standard VLM architectures and text-based training.
AI.conclusion: VLM3 demonstrates that standard vision-language models can serve as effective and scalable 3D learners without complex task-specific model designs. By focusing on focal length unification, text-based pixel reference, and data mixture/scaling, it matches or exceeds expert 3D vision systems across multiple tasks.

title: Generating Graph-like Rules for Knowledge Graph Reasoning via Diffusion Models
summary: Logical rules constitute a cornerstone of knowledge graph (KG) reasoning, valued for their interpretability and ability to model relational patterns. However, existing rule mining methods predominantly focus on simple chain-like rules and therefore neglect the richer relational information encoded in graph-like structures, such as cycles and branches. This limitation is further exacerbated by computational bottlenecks caused by the combinatorial explosion of the search space, which is especially challenging for graph-like rules. Meanwhile, generative approaches such as diffusion models, despite their success in other domains, can not be directly applied to rule mining because their training objectives are not aligned with the goal of learning high-quality rules, and non-differentiable KG rule quality metrics cannot directly guide model optimization. To address these limitations, we propose GRiD, a framework that reformulates graph-like rule discovery as a discrete generative process conditioned on the target relation. GRiD employs a two-phase training strategy. First, supervised pre-training enables GRiD to capture structural priors from subgraphs sampled from the KG meta-graph. Subsequently, reinforcement learning is applied to fine-tune GRiD through policy gradient optimization guided directly by non-differentiable rule-quality metrics. Experiments on six benchmark datasets show that GRiD achieves competitive performance on KG completion tasks. Ablation studies confirm the efficiency and robustness of GRiD and further show that graph-like rules complement chain-like rules in KG completion. Our codes and datasets are available in https://github.com/Haoxiang-Cheng/GRiD

AI.tldr: GRiD treats graph-like KG rule mining as conditional discrete generation, learns structure with supervised pre-training, then improves rule quality with reinforcement learning, producing competitive KG completion results and showing graph-like rules add value beyond chain-like ones.
AI.motivation: Existing KG rule mining methods mainly focus on simple chain-like rules and miss richer graph-like structures such as cycles and branches. Directly extending search-based mining is computationally difficult due to combinatorial explosion, while standard generative models like diffusion models are not naturally aligned with rule-quality optimization.
AI.method: The paper proposes GRiD, a framework for graph-like rule mining. It first performs supervised pre-training on subgraphs sampled from the KG meta-graph to learn structural priors, then applies reinforcement learning with policy gradient to optimize generation using non-differentiable rule-quality metrics as rewards.
AI.result: Across six benchmark datasets, GRiD achieves competitive results on knowledge graph completion. Ablation studies show the framework is efficient and robust, and that graph-like rules provide complementary value to chain-like rules.
AI.conclusion: GRiD demonstrates that graph-like rule discovery for knowledge graphs can be effectively modeled as a target-relation-conditioned discrete generative process, and that combining supervised pre-training with reinforcement learning improves the quality of mined rules and yields competitive KG completion performance.

title: Bounded Behavioral Indistinguishability for Black-Box LLM Distillation
summary:
Black-box LLM distillation is usually evaluated as an output-matching problem: a student is considered successful when its responses are semantically similar to, or task-consistent with, those of a teacher. However, output similarity does not imply that the student is behaviorally indistinguishable from the model it imitates. We introduce bounded behavioral indistinguishability, formalized as $(ε,q,t,\mathbb{A})$-behavioral indistinguishability over an explicit prompt distribution, where $ε$ bounds distinguishing advantage, $q$ bounds oracle queries, $t$ bounds computation, and $\mathbb{A}$ denotes the adversary class.
  We instantiate this notion on Qwen and Llama teacher-student pairs using a controlled $5,000$-prompt behavioral probe suite. For each family, we compare the teacher with both the base student and the LoRA-distilled student, measuring whether distillation reduces distinguishability rather than merely improving similarity. LoRA raises semantic similarity from $0.788$ to $0.862$ for Qwen and from $0.814$ to $0.874$ for Llama. Yet adversarial evaluation reveals remaining behavioral differences: learned discriminators retain nonzero advantage, and pairwise category analysis shows artifacts concentrated in style/format, robustness, and domain-technical prompts. A pairwise teacher-identification adversary confirms this trend. With a different-family Llama judge and A/B-swap consistency filtering, Qwen distinguishing advantage drops from $0.158$ for the base student to $0.081$ after LoRA distillation. Query-budget experiments show that disagreement-guided acquisition does not consistently outperform stratified random sampling, indicating that coverage and diversity remain strong baselines. Our results show that semantic fidelity is useful but insufficient: black-box LLM distillation requires bounded, adversarial, and category-aware evaluation.

AI.tldr: 论文提出“有界行为不可区分性”来评估黑盒LLM蒸馏，不再只看输出像不像。实验表明LoRA让学生更像老师，但还远未达到行为上不可区分；真正可靠的评估应包含对抗式测试、查询预算和类别级分析。 / The paper introduces bounded behavioral indistinguishability for evaluating black-box LLM distillation instead of relying only on output similarity. Experiments show LoRA makes students more similar to teachers, but not behaviorally indistinguishable; robust evaluation needs adversarial testing, query budgets, and category-level analysis.
AI.motivation: 现有黑盒蒸馏通常只看输出匹配或任务一致性，但这不足以判断学生模型是否真正像老师模型那样行为一致。论文动机是建立一个更严格、更可操作的评估标准，衡量蒸馏是否真的降低了模型被区分开的可能性。 / Existing black-box distillation is typically judged by output matching or task consistency, which is insufficient to determine whether the student truly behaves like the teacher. The motivation is to provide a stricter and operational evaluation criterion that measures whether distillation actually reduces distinguishability.
AI.method: 定义了在显式提示分布上的(ε,q,t,A)-behavioral indistinguishability，其中ε是区分优势上界，q是查询预算，t是计算预算，A是对手类别。作者在Qwen和Llama师生对上，用5000条prompt行为探针，比较teacher、base student和LoRA蒸馏student；结合学习型判别器、pairwise teacher-identification adversary、A/B-swap一致性过滤，以及查询预算实验来测量可区分性。 / The authors formalize (ε,q,t,A)-behavioral indistinguishability over an explicit prompt distribution, where ε bounds distinguishing advantage, q bounds queries, t bounds computation, and A specifies the adversary class. They instantiate it on Qwen and Llama teacher-student pairs using a 5,000-prompt behavioral probe suite, comparing teacher, base student, and LoRA-distilled student via learned discriminators, a pairwise teacher-identification adversary, A/B-swap consistency filtering, and query-budget experiments.
AI.result: LoRA蒸馏显著提高语义相似度：Qwen从0.788到0.862，Llama从0.814到0.874。但对抗评估显示仍存在可检测的行为差异，尤其集中在风格/格式、鲁棒性和技术领域prompt上。对Qwen，在异家族Llama judge和A/B-swap过滤下，区分优势从base student的0.158降到LoRA后的0.081。查询预算实验还表明，基于分歧的主动采样并未稳定优于分层随机采样。 / LoRA distillation substantially improves semantic similarity: from 0.788 to 0.862 for Qwen and from 0.814 to 0.874 for Llama. However, adversarial evaluation still finds detectable behavioral gaps, especially in style/format, robustness, and technical-domain prompts. For Qwen, under a cross-family Llama judge with A/B-swap consistency filtering, distinguishing advantage drops from 0.158 for the base student to 0.081 after LoRA distillation. Query-budget experiments further show disagreement-guided acquisition does not consistently beat stratified random sampling.
AI.conclusion: 语义相似度提升并不等于行为上不可区分。该论文提出有界行为不可区分性框架，证明黑盒LLM蒸馏需要结合对抗式、带预算、按类别的行为评估。 / Improved semantic similarity does not guarantee behavioral indistinguishability. The paper proposes a bounded behavioral indistinguishability framework and shows black-box LLM distillation must be evaluated with adversarial, budgeted, category-aware behavioral tests.

title: Auditing LLM Benchmarks with Item Response Theory
summary: LLM benchmark labels are frozen at release and silently propagated into downstream benchmarks, errors and all. We introduce an Item Response Theory-based indicator that surfaces likely mislabels at 95% precision in the top 200 examples across seven preference and multiple-choice benchmarks using responses from 114 models, outperforming a supervised classifier. We trace these errors to mechanical labeling heuristics, upstream annotation mistakes inherited unchanged from source datasets, and fundamentally ambiguous items without a defensible single label. The same model fit reveals that reward models specialize in stylistic preference rather than factual knowledge, and identifies one frontier reward model that agrees with detected mislabels at 78% accuracy versus 38% for its peers, consistent with benchmark contamination or benchmark-specific over-optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper uses IRT on many-model benchmark responses to find likely benchmark mislabels with high precision, shows where those errors come from, and reveals signs that some reward models may be benchmark-specificly overfit or contaminated.
AI.motivation: Benchmark labels are fixed at release and propagated downstream without systematic auditing, so labeling mistakes and ambiguous items can distort evaluation and model comparison.
AI.method: The paper fits an IRT-based indicator over responses from 114 models across seven preference and multiple-choice benchmarks, then ranks examples by likelihood of being mislabeled and evaluates precision in the top suspicious items. It also compares this approach against a supervised classifier and analyzes model-specific agreement patterns.
AI.result: The IRT-based indicator reaches 95% precision in the top 200 flagged examples across seven benchmarks and outperforms a supervised classifier. The analysis attributes errors to heuristic labeling, inherited upstream annotation mistakes, and intrinsically ambiguous items. It also shows reward models focus more on stylistic preference than factual knowledge, and one frontier reward model matches detected mislabels at 78% accuracy versus 38% for peers.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM benchmarks contain non-trivial label errors and ambiguous items that can be detected effectively with an Item Response Theory (IRT)-based signal; benchmark artifacts may also induce reward-model over-optimization or contamination.

title: Prior Availability in Industrial Visual Sim-to-Real: A Review of CAD-Guided and CAD-Unavailable Regimes
comment: Review article; 103 references; 9 main figures; empirical anchors on T-LESS/BOP, MVTec AD, and VisA
summary: Industrial visual sim-to-real is often described as transferring from synthetic images to real images, but industrial deployment usually involves a broader mismatch between available evidence and required decisions. A system may be built from CAD renderings, simulated RGB-D observations, normal reference images, synthetic defects, pretrained feature spaces, or language prompts, yet deployed under different sensors, lighting, materials, fixtures, calibration, production variation, and rare defect modes. This review reframes industrial visual sim-to-real as a domain-gap problem organized by prior availability. We distinguish CAD-available settings, where explicit object geometry can support rendering, calibration, pose estimation, segmentation, and test-time geometric verification; CAD-unavailable settings, where geometry is replaced by normal-reference appearance, feature distributions, teacher-student residuals, synthetic anomaly assumptions, foundation features, or vision-language priors; and boundary-prior settings, where approximate models, templates, reference views, or semantic correspondences preserve only part of the CAD role. This framing connects CAD-based detection and 6D pose-estimation literature with industrial anomaly and surface-inspection literature that is usually reviewed separately. To make the taxonomy concrete, we use empirical anchors on T-LESS/BOP, MVTec AD, and VisA. The anchors show that CAD render count alone does not close transfer; source-distribution design, detector capacity, and small real calibration can matter more. They also show that CAD at test time creates a distinct verification channel through mask, pose, and depth consistency, whereas CAD-unavailable inspection relies on calibrated normality and feature deviation. The review therefore argues against a single cross-task leaderboard and instead asks what prior grounds the deployment decision.

AI.tldr: This review redefines industrial visual sim-to-real as a prior-dependent domain-gap problem: CAD enables geometry-based verification, missing CAD shifts methods toward normality and feature-deviation modeling, and evaluation should be organized by deployment prior rather than one cross-task leaderboard.
AI.motivation: Existing descriptions of industrial sim-to-real are too narrow because real deployment gaps involve not only image realism but also mismatches in sensors, lighting, materials, calibration, production variation, and defect rarity. A broader framework is needed to explain how different priors support different industrial decisions.
AI.method: The paper proposes a taxonomy based on prior availability: CAD-available, CAD-unavailable, and boundary-prior settings. It connects literature across CAD-based detection/6D pose estimation and anomaly/surface inspection, and grounds the taxonomy with empirical anchors on T-LESS/BOP, MVTec AD, and VisA.
AI.result: The analysis shows that increasing CAD render count alone is insufficient to close the transfer gap; source-distribution design, model capacity, and limited real calibration often matter more. It also shows that CAD provides a distinct test-time geometric verification channel, while CAD-unavailable settings depend on modeling normality and detecting feature deviations.
AI.conclusion: The review argues that industrial visual sim-to-real should be framed as a domain-gap problem defined by what prior information is available at deployment, rather than as a simple synthetic-to-real image transfer problem or a single unified benchmark.

title: Learning Agent-Compatible Context Management for Long-Horizon Tasks
summary: LLM agents increasingly face long-horizon tasks such as web search and deep research in real-world applications, where accumulated context can cause long-context degradation and reasoning failures. Prior work mitigates this through context management with agent-side context control or fixed strategies such as summarization, which require training the agent itself for adaptation - making it impractical for closed-source agents and ignoring that different agents may require different strategies. We introduce Adaptive Context Management (AdaCoM), which trains an external LLM to manage the context of a frozen agent through flexible modification actions and end-to-end reinforcement learning. Across diverse agents on web search and deep research benchmarks, AdaCoM substantially improves performance by preserving task constraints and progress while pruning stale content. The learned strategies reveal a Fidelity-Reliability Trade-off: agents with higher vanilla ReAct performance benefit from higher-fidelity context preservation, whereas lower-performing agents require more aggressive compression to stay within a reliable reasoning regime. Transfer experiments show that AdaCoM generalizes most effectively across agents with similar capability (measured by vanilla ReAct performance), suggesting a practical path toward reusable context managers for agent systems.

AI.tldr: AdaCoM trains an external LLM, via reinforcement learning, to adaptively rewrite a frozen agent’s context, improving long-horizon performance and revealing that optimal context fidelity depends on the agent’s baseline capability.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon agent tasks accumulate large context, causing long-context degradation and reasoning failures. Existing context-management approaches often rely on fixed heuristics or require training the agent, which is impractical for closed-source agents and may not generalize across agents with different needs.
AI.method: The paper proposes Adaptive Context Management (AdaCoM), which trains an external LLM to manage the context of a frozen agent. It performs flexible context modification actions and is optimized end-to-end with reinforcement learning, without requiring modification or retraining of the target agent itself.
AI.result: Across web search and deep research benchmarks and multiple agent backbones, AdaCoM substantially improves performance. The learned policies expose a fidelity-reliability trade-off: stronger agents benefit from preserving higher-fidelity context, while weaker agents do better with more aggressive compression. Transfer works best across agents with similar vanilla ReAct capability.
AI.conclusion: AdaCoM shows that an external, trainable context manager can substantially improve frozen LLM agents on long-horizon tasks by adaptively preserving important constraints/progress and pruning stale context. The best transfer occurs between agents with similar baseline capability, indicating reusable context managers are feasible within capability bands.

title: VeriGate: Verifier-Gated Step-Level Supervision for GRPO
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is an effective recipe for training reasoning models with verifier-based outcome rewards, but its supervision is sparse: when all sampled trajectories for a prompt receive the same verifier reward, the group-relative advantage collapses to zero and learning stalls. Outcome-only rewards also provide no step-level credit assignment, limiting exploration and making it harder to learn robust reasoning. We present VeriGate (Verifier-Gated Step-Level GRPO), a verifier-gated extension of GRPO that addresses these limitations with three design choices. First, VeriGate keeps the verifier in charge whenever verifier rewards induce a meaningful preference among sampled trajectories, and uses process supervision only when verifier rewards are degenerate. Second, instead of collapsing Process Reward Model (PRM) step scores into a single trajectory reward, VeriGate converts them into future-cumulated rewards to assign continuation-aware credit. Third, VeriGate transforms these rewards into group-normalized token-level advantages, restoring informative gradients and fine-grained credit assignment while remaining less susceptible to reward hacking than methods that optimize aggregated PRM scores. Empirically, training on MATH with 1.5B and 7B Qwen2.5-Instruct models and evaluating on six reasoning benchmarks, VeriGate improves average accuracy by about 20% and 12% for 1.5B and 7B models respectively, substantially reduces zero-gradient failures, decreases reward-hacking behavior, and improves reasoning quality relative to outcome-only GRPO and PRM-as-outcome baselines.

AI.tldr: VeriGate fixes GRPO’s sparse-reward problem by using verifier signals when informative and step-level PRM credit when not, yielding better token-level learning, less reward hacking, and significantly higher reasoning accuracy.
AI.motivation: Standard GRPO with verifier-based outcome rewards suffers from sparse supervision: when sampled trajectories for a prompt receive identical verifier rewards, the relative advantage becomes zero and learning stalls. Outcome-only rewards also lack step-level credit assignment, limiting exploration and robust reasoning learning.
AI.method: The method introduces three components: (1) use verifier rewards when they provide meaningful trajectory preferences, but fall back to process supervision when verifier rewards are degenerate; (2) convert PRM step scores into future-cumulated rewards for continuation-aware credit assignment; and (3) transform these rewards into group-normalized token-level advantages for fine-grained optimization.
AI.result: On MATH training with Qwen2.5-Instruct 1.5B and 7B models and evaluation on six reasoning benchmarks, VeriGate improves average accuracy by about 20% and 12% respectively, substantially reduces zero-gradient failures, decreases reward hacking, and improves reasoning quality compared with outcome-only GRPO and PRM-as-outcome baselines.
AI.conclusion: VeriGate extends GRPO with verifier-gated step-level credit assignment, avoiding zero-advantage collapse under degenerate verifier rewards and improving robustness and reasoning quality over outcome-only and PRM-as-outcome baselines.

title: ReGuLaR: Relation-Grounded Latent Reasoning for Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has significantly improved the reasoning ability of large vision-language models (LVLMs) by verbalizing intermediate reasoning steps in natural language. However, such discrete textual rationales are often insufficient for encoding continuous visual evidence. Recent work addresses this limitation by moving reasoning into continuous latent space. Despite promising progress, existing methods leave latent reasoning insufficiently connected to the compositional and relational structure of visual evidence. To address this gap, we introduce ReGuLaR, a relation grounded latent reasoning framework that explicitly grounds latent states in these critical yet overlooked visual evidence. ReGuLaR uses a training-time ReGFormer to focus latent reasoning on question-relevant objects and inter-object relations, while at inference time the model reasons and generates answers without invoking the ReGFormer. To support training ReGuLaR, we construct RGROUNDING-351K, a real-world vision-language dataset annotated with key object bounding boxes and inter-object relations. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks show that ReGuLaR consistently outperforms existing approaches and achieves state-of-the-art performance. We include our code in the submission and will release the code and training data publicly upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: 中文：这篇论文提出ReGuLaR，把潜在推理显式绑定到图像中的关键物体及其关系上，并通过新数据集RGROUNDING-351K训练，最终让LVLM在多项视觉推理任务上取得更强表现。 English: The paper introduces ReGuLaR, a latent reasoning framework grounded in key objects and their relations, trained with the new RGROUNDING-351K dataset, leading to stronger LVLM reasoning performance on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: 中文：现有CoT文本推理难以表达连续视觉证据，而已有潜在推理方法又未能充分建模视觉证据中的组合性与关系结构，因此需要一种关系驱动的潜在推理机制。 English: Textual CoT is limited for representing continuous visual evidence, and prior latent reasoning methods insufficiently capture compositional and relational visual structure, motivating a relation-grounded latent reasoning approach.
AI.method: 中文：提出ReGuLaR框架，在训练时使用ReGFormer将潜在状态对齐到关键目标框和目标间关系；推理时无需调用ReGFormer，模型直接进行潜在推理并生成答案。同时构建了带有目标框和关系标注的数据集RGROUNDING-351K用于训练。 English: The paper proposes ReGuLaR, which uses a training-time ReGFormer to align latent states with salient object boxes and inter-object relations; at inference, the model reasons in latent space and answers without ReGFormer. It is trained with a new dataset, RGROUNDING-351K, annotated with object boxes and relations.
AI.result: 中文：在多个视觉语言推理基准上，ReGuLaR稳定优于现有方法，并取得最先进性能。 English: ReGuLaR consistently outperforms existing approaches on diverse vision-language benchmarks and reaches state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: 中文：ReGuLaR通过将潜在推理显式锚定到与问题相关的目标及其关系，显著提升了视觉语言推理性能，并在多个基准上达到SOTA。 English: ReGuLaR shows that explicitly grounding latent reasoning in question-relevant objects and inter-object relations substantially improves vision-language reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art results across benchmarks.

title: PReMISE: Policy Rubrics as Measurement Specifications for LLM Judges
summary: LLM judges are increasingly used to evaluate open-ended responses, but their scores depend strongly on the rubrics that condition them. A vague rubric asking for a response to be ``helpful and factual'' can reward polished answers that invent facts or violate user intent. We treat reusable rubrics as measurement specifications: changing the rubric changes the response quality measurement induced by a fixed judge. We introduce PReMISE, a framework that, given pairwise human-preference data, (i) discovers a policy-level rubric set, and (ii) audits any rubric set under LLM-judge use along four axes: structural adequacy, reliability, preference fit, and adversarial robustness. Across rubric sources no raw source is simultaneously reliable, preference-predictive, and adversarially robust; and high inter-rater agreement does not imply low exploitability. PReMISE is the only rubric source to score non-trivially on applicability, specificity, and effective dimensionality simultaneously. We contribute two audit-targeted repair operations: preference-rank selection raises judge accuracy on paired responses from $65.0\%$ to $68.6\%$, competitive with the strongest rubric-discovery baselines and leading on two of three judges in our cross-judge sweep; reliability-constrained refinement reduces the rate at which exploit responses receive high scores from $46.4\%$ to $36.0\%$ with little change in inter-judge agreement ($α{=}.531\to.519$).

AI.tldr: 中文：这篇论文研究“LLM裁判为什么会被rubric带偏”。作者提出PReMISE，把rubric当作评价规范来自动发现、系统审计并定向修复，结果证明比起只看一致性，更应同时看偏好拟合和抗攻击性。 English: This paper studies how rubrics steer LLM judges. It proposes PReMISE to discover, audit, and repair rubrics as measurement specifications, showing that agreement alone is insufficient without preference alignment and adversarial robustness.
AI.motivation: 中文：现有LLM judge常依赖模糊rubric，例如“helpful and factual”，这会奖励表面流畅但事实虚构或偏离用户意图的回答。作者希望把rubric从随意提示提升为可复用、可审计、可修复的评价规范。 English: Existing LLM judges often rely on vague rubrics such as “helpful and factual,” which can reward fluent but hallucinated or misaligned responses. The motivation is to treat rubrics not as informal prompts but as reusable, auditable, and repairable measurement specifications.
AI.method: 中文：提出PReMISE框架，基于成对人类偏好数据完成两件事：1）发现策略层面的rubric集合；2）从结构充分性、可靠性、偏好拟合、对抗鲁棒性四个维度审计任意rubric集合。此外还设计两种修复操作：preference-rank selection 与 reliability-constrained refinement。 English: The authors introduce PReMISE, which uses pairwise human-preference data to (1) discover a policy-level rubric set and (2) audit any rubric set across four axes: structural adequacy, reliability, preference fit, and adversarial robustness. They also propose two repair operations: preference-rank selection and reliability-constrained refinement.
AI.result: 中文：实验表明，没有任何原始rubric来源能同时兼顾可靠性、偏好预测能力和对抗鲁棒性；高一致性也不代表不易被攻击。PReMISE是唯一在applicability、specificity和effective dimensionality上都取得非平凡表现的rubric来源。修复后，preference-rank selection将成对回答判别准确率从65.0%提升到68.6%；reliability-constrained refinement将对抗样本获得高分的比例从46.4%降到36.0%，且评审一致性仅小幅变化（α=.531→.519）。 English: Empirically, no raw rubric source is simultaneously reliable, preference-predictive, and adversarially robust; strong inter-rater agreement does not imply low exploitability. PReMISE is the only source scoring non-trivially on applicability, specificity, and effective dimensionality together. After repair, preference-rank selection improves paired-response judge accuracy from 65.0% to 68.6%, while reliability-constrained refinement lowers the exploit-high-score rate from 46.4% to 36.0% with only a small agreement change (α=.531→.519).
AI.conclusion: 中文：论文认为，用于驱动LLM裁判的rubric本质上是“测量规范”，不同rubric会显著改变评分结果；PReMISE能够系统发现并审计rubric，并通过修复操作同时改善偏好拟合与对抗鲁棒性。 English: The paper concludes that rubrics act as measurement specifications for LLM judges, materially changing what quality is measured; PReMISE can discover and audit rubrics systematically, and targeted repairs improve both preference alignment and adversarial robustness.

title: A Unified Framework for Gradient Aggregation in Multi-Objective Optimization
summary: Many machine learning problems involve multiple inherent trade-offs that are best addressed by gradient-based multi-objective optimization (MOO) algorithms. Existing methods are often proposed with various motivations, analyzed case by case, and differ algorithmically in how the component gradients are aggregated at each step. In this work, we develop a unifying framework for gradient aggregation in MOO, establishing (optimal) rates of convergence to Pareto stationarity, the standard measure of performance in MOO. Central to our analysis is a sufficient alignment condition, from which we derive a theorem showing that non-conflicting directions, when chosen within the convex hull of gradients, form a fundamental sufficient condition for convergence. We further show that feasibility can be ensured through projection onto the dual cone, broadening the scope of methods that admit convergence guarantees. In parallel, we present a primal optimization perspective of gradient aggregation that encompasses established algorithms, clarifies their theoretical relationships, and enables the design of new variants. As an illustration, we introduce capped MGDA, derived from a CVaR-based formulation, and demonstrate its robustness in adversarial federated learning. Finally, we validate our theory through experiments on synthetic problems and practical benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper unifies gradient aggregation methods for multi-objective optimization, proves broad convergence guarantees, and introduces a new robust variant, capped MGDA, that works well in adversarial federated learning.
AI.motivation: Existing gradient-based MOO methods are fragmented: they are motivated differently, analyzed separately, and use different gradient aggregation rules. The paper aims to unify these methods theoretically, clarify when they converge, and provide a principled basis for designing new algorithms.
AI.method: The paper develops a unifying theoretical and primal-optimization framework for gradient aggregation in MOO, proves convergence via a sufficient alignment condition, characterizes non-conflicting directions in the convex hull of gradients as sufficient for convergence, uses projection onto the dual cone to ensure feasibility, and derives a new CVaR-based variant called capped MGDA.
AI.result: The work establishes optimal convergence rates to Pareto stationarity, broadens the class of methods with guarantees through dual-cone projection, unifies established algorithms under a primal view, introduces capped MGDA, and empirically shows robustness in adversarial federated learning as well as consistency with theory on synthetic and practical benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A unified framework for gradient aggregation in gradient-based multi-objective optimization yields convergence guarantees to Pareto stationarity under a sufficient alignment condition, and this perspective also motivates new robust algorithms such as capped MGDA.

title: Generalistic or Specific Embeddings, Which is Better? An Empirical Study on Search for Clinical Coding in Non-English Languages
summary: Sentence-embedding models for semantic search are overwhelmingly developed and evaluated on English corpora. When applied to clinical retrieval in other languages -- particularly retrieval of ICD-10-CM / CIE-10 codes -- recall degrades in ways often masked by aggregate benchmarks. We study whether large generative language models can serve as data factories to close this gap. We build a two-stage retriever (bi-encoder followed by cross-encoder reranker), fine-tuned from a Spanish biomedical encoder (PlanTL-GOB-ES/bsc-bio-ehr-es) on Gemini-generated synthetic data covering English, Spanish, Catalan, Italian, Portuguese and French, and evaluate against BioBERT-ST and the un-tuned Spanish encoder. The bi-encoder alone matches BioBERT-ST on MRR (0.876 vs. 0.866) and overtakes it on R@3 (0.650 vs. 0.626) and R@5 (0.804 vs. 0.790) without English biomedical pretraining. Adding a cross-encoder reranker lifts aggregate R@5 to 0.822 and dominates on four of five languages (+0.017 Spanish, +0.033 Catalan, +0.018 French, +0.037 Portuguese) at the cost of a small English regression. The trade-off is clinically acceptable: Portuguese reaches R@5 = 0.829 vs. BioBERT-ST's 0.714. Contributions: an open recipe for building domain-specific medical retrievers from LLM-generated data; quantification of the learning gain (MRR 0.755 to 0.876, +15.9% with ~19,500 synthetic pairs); and a characterisation of where gains concentrate by language and rank.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that LLMs can act as scalable data generators for multilingual medical retrieval. By fine-tuning a Spanish biomedical encoder on ~19.5k synthetic multilingual pairs and adding reranking, the system beats a strong baseline on most non-English languages and delivers clinically meaningful recall gains.
AI.motivation: Most sentence-embedding retrieval models are built and benchmarked mainly on English data, so their weaknesses in multilingual clinical retrieval, particularly ICD-10-CM/CIE-10 code retrieval, are often obscured. The paper aims to close this non-English performance gap using synthetic data generated by large language models.
AI.method: The paper builds a two-stage retrieval pipeline: a bi-encoder for initial semantic retrieval and a cross-encoder for reranking. Both are fine-tuned from the Spanish biomedical encoder PlanTL-GOB-ES/bsc-bio-ehr-es using Gemini-generated synthetic training pairs spanning English, Spanish, Catalan, Italian, Portuguese, and French. Performance is compared against BioBERT-ST and the untuned Spanish encoder.
AI.result: The fine-tuned bi-encoder reaches MRR 0.876 versus BioBERT-ST’s 0.866, and improves R@3 to 0.650 versus 0.626 and R@5 to 0.804 versus 0.790. Adding a cross-encoder reranker raises aggregate R@5 to 0.822 and outperforms the baseline in four of five languages, including gains of +0.017 in Spanish, +0.033 in Catalan, +0.018 in French, and +0.037 in Portuguese. Portuguese achieves R@5 = 0.829 versus BioBERT-ST’s 0.714. Training gain is quantified from MRR 0.755 to 0.876 using about 19,500 synthetic pairs.
AI.conclusion: LLM-generated synthetic multilingual biomedical training data can substantially improve non-English clinical code retrieval, especially when used to fine-tune a Spanish biomedical bi-encoder and paired with a cross-encoder reranker. The approach is effective across several Romance languages, with only a small trade-off on English.

title: Crafter: A Multi-Agent Harness for Editable Scientific Figure Generation from Diverse Inputs
summary: Scientific figures are among the most effective means of communicating complex research ideas, yet producing publication-quality illustrations remains one of the most labor-intensive parts of paper preparation. Existing automated systems each target a single figure type under text-only input, leaving the diversity of types and conditions researchers actually use unaddressed; their raster outputs further cannot be locally revised. Because scientific figures are structured compositions of discrete semantic components, the localized errors generators produce on such layouts demand not a stronger backbone but a harness. We instantiate this harness in two complementary systems: Crafter, a multi-agent harness for figure generation that generalizes across figure types and input conditions without architectural changes, and CraftEditor, which applies the same pattern to convert raster outputs into editable SVGs. Moreover, we introduce CraftBench, a benchmark spanning three figure types and four input conditions with human quality annotation. Experiments show that Crafter substantially outperforms both standalone generators and the agentic baseline on PaperBanana-Bench and CraftBench, with ablations confirming each component's independent contribution; CraftEditor faithfully converts outputs into editable SVGs that surpass all baselines. Our code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/HaozheZhao/Crafter.

AI.tldr: 作者提出一个用于科学图生成与编辑的multi-agent框架：Crafter负责生成，CraftEditor负责把位图转成可编辑SVG，CraftBench负责评测。核心贡献是用harness协调已有生成能力，以适配多图类型、多输入条件，并显著提升质量和可编辑性。 / TL;DR: The paper introduces a multi-agent framework for scientific figure creation and editing: Crafter generates figures, CraftEditor converts raster outputs into editable SVGs, and CraftBench evaluates them. The key idea is to harness existing generators with structured agent coordination to support diverse figure types and inputs while improving quality and editability.
AI.motivation: 动机是现有自动化科学绘图系统通常只支持单一图形类型和text-only输入，无法覆盖研究者真实使用场景中的多样类型与条件；同时其raster输出难以局部修改，而科学图本质上由离散语义组件组成，错误常是局部性的，因此需要一个能够约束和纠正生成过程的harness。 / The motivation is that existing automated figure systems usually support only one figure type and text-only input, failing to cover the diversity of real research workflows; moreover, their raster outputs are hard to revise locally. Since scientific figures are structured compositions of discrete semantic components and errors are often localized, the problem calls for a harness rather than merely a stronger backbone.
AI.method: 方法上，作者构建了一个不依赖修改底层生成架构的multi-agent harness。Crafter用于跨图类型、跨输入条件的科学图生成；CraftEditor将raster输出转换为可编辑SVG；并提出CraftBench作为覆盖3类图形、4种输入条件且带有人类质量标注的评测基准。 / Methodologically, the authors build a multi-agent harness without changing the underlying generator architecture. Crafter handles figure generation across figure types and input conditions; CraftEditor converts raster outputs into editable SVGs; and CraftBench provides evaluation over three figure types and four input conditions with human annotations.
AI.result: 实验结果表明，Crafter在PaperBanana-Bench和CraftBench上明显优于独立生成器和agentic baseline，消融实验验证了各组件的独立贡献；CraftEditor在将结果转换为可编辑SVG方面也优于所有基线。 / Results show that Crafter substantially outperforms standalone generators and the agentic baseline on both PaperBanana-Bench and CraftBench, ablations confirm the independent contribution of each component, and CraftEditor surpasses all baselines in producing faithful editable SVGs.
AI.conclusion: 提出了Crafter、CraftEditor和CraftBench，证明基于multi-agent harness的方法能在多种科学图类型与输入条件下显著提升生成质量，并将结果可靠地转为可编辑SVG。 / The paper concludes that a multi-agent harness, instantiated as Crafter and CraftEditor, substantially improves scientific figure generation across figure types and input conditions, while enabling reliable conversion to editable SVGs.

title: Planner-Centric Reinforcement Learning for Deep Research with Structure-Aware Reward
summary: Deep research tasks require LLMs to plan what to investigate, retrieve evidence, and synthesize long-form answers across multiple branches of inquiry. Existing training paradigms either rely on short-form verifiable QA as a proxy or optimize monolithic long trajectories, which makes planning and execution difficult to disentangle and yields weak credit assignment for the planning process. We propose DecomposeR, a planner-centric deep research framework that represents research plans as typed directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), allowing planning to be made explicit, structured, and rewardable. We train a Qwen3-8B model in two stages: planner reinforcement learning (RL) first learns graph structure and query decomposition to improve research planning, and answerer reinforcement learning (RL) then learns branch-level execution and final synthesis conditioned on the learned plan. By assigning rewards to explicit planner tokens and structured components rather than to a flat trajectory, DecomposeR enables finer-grained optimization of planning while reducing the ambiguity of end-to-end training. Experiments show that DecomposeR-8B improves over strong comparable open baselines by 5.1-8.0 points on popular long-form benchmarks due to improved planning and answering capabilities.

AI.tldr: DecomposeR trains LLM deep research in two stages around an explicit DAG-based planner, which gives better credit assignment for planning and improves long-form benchmark scores by 5.1-8.0 points.
AI.motivation: Prior deep research training either uses short-form verifiable QA as a proxy or trains monolithic long trajectories end-to-end. Both approaches blur planning and execution, making credit assignment for planning weak and limiting optimization of long-horizon research behavior.
AI.method: The paper proposes DecomposeR, a planner-centric framework that models research plans as typed directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). A Qwen3-8B model is trained in two RL stages: first, planner RL learns graph structure and query decomposition; second, answerer RL learns branch-level evidence gathering, execution, and final synthesis conditioned on the learned plan.
AI.result: On popular long-form benchmarks, DecomposeR-8B outperforms strong comparable open baselines by 5.1 to 8.0 points, with gains attributed to better planning and answering.
AI.conclusion: DecomposeR shows that making research planning explicit as a typed DAG and training planning separately from execution improves deep research performance, yielding stronger long-form reasoning and answer synthesis than comparable open baselines.

title: DisjunctiveNet: Neural Symbolic Learning via Differentiable Convexified Optimization Layers
summary: Many learning tasks in science and engineering are characterized by sparse datasets, which limits the effectiveness of purely data-driven approaches. At the same time, these problems are often accompanied by rich domain knowledge derived from physical laws, operational requirements, and expert heuristics. Such knowledge is frequently expressed as rules involving logical propositions and linear inequalities. Existing neuro-symbolic methods typically enforce these rules approximately through soft penalties, assume input-independent rules when designing specialized architectures, or rely on non-differentiable post-processing at inference time to achieve hard constraint satisfaction. While recent advances in differentiable optimization layers enable end-to-end feasibility enforcement within neural networks, extending these approaches to logical or mixed-integer rules remains challenging due to inherent nonconvexity. In this work, we propose a unified end-to-end framework for enforcing hard, input-dependent mixed integer linear constraints within neural networks. Our approach represents rules as disjunctive constraints and applies hierarchical convex relaxations to obtain convex hull formulations. These relaxations yield tractable linear constraints that can be embedded as differentiable optimization layers while enabling exact rule satisfaction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework on real-world datasets, achieving perfect rule satisfaction and strong predictive performance.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic framework that embeds hard, input-dependent mixed-integer linear rules into neural networks via convex relaxations and differentiable optimization layers, delivering exact rule satisfaction and strong predictive results.
AI.motivation: The motivation is that many scientific and engineering learning problems have sparse data but rich structured prior knowledge. Existing neuro-symbolic approaches either enforce rules only approximately, assume fixed rule structures, or require non-differentiable post-processing, making exact and trainable enforcement of logical or mixed-integer rules difficult.
AI.method: The method represents domain rules as disjunctive mixed-integer linear constraints, then applies hierarchical convex relaxations to derive convex hull formulations. These are converted into tractable linear constraints and embedded into the network as differentiable optimization layers for end-to-end training and inference.
AI.result: On real-world datasets, the framework achieves perfect rule satisfaction while maintaining strong predictive performance, showing that exact constraint enforcement can be practical in end-to-end neural models.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that hard, input-dependent mixed-integer linear rules can be enforced exactly within neural networks by converting disjunctive rule structures into tractable convex formulations embedded as differentiable optimization layers, achieving both exact feasibility and strong prediction accuracy.

title: Refining Word-Based Grammatical Error Annotation for L2 Korean
summary: Korean grammatical error correction (K-GEC) presents a structural mismatch between word-based evaluation and the morpheme-level locus of many learner errors. Postpositions and verbal endings are bound to lexical hosts, but they encode grammatical relations that must be represented in correction and evaluation. This paper refines word-based grammatical error annotation for L2 Korean by addressing three connected problems in existing resources: surface target realization, Korean-specific edit annotation, and single-reference evaluation. We reconstruct target sentences from the National Institute of Korean Language (NIKL) L2 corpus under morphologically constrained realization rules and convert its morpheme-level annotations into word-level \texttt{m2} edits.
