AI.result: The study identifies evidence of uncertainty alignment in model behavior and representations, tests its strength across several datasets and task formats, and characterizes how instruction fine-tuning changes both alignment and calibration.
AI.conclusion: Large language models exhibit measurable human-similar uncertainty signals in both overt outputs and internal activations, and these signals can coexist with calibration; instruction fine-tuning affects these properties in distinct ways.

title: Text-guided Feature Disentanglement for Cross-modal Gait Recognition
summary: Gait recognition is a biometric technique that identifies individuals based on their walking patterns, offering advantages in long-range, non-intrusive scenarios. However, real-world scenarios often involve heterogeneous sensing modalities such as LiDAR and RGB cameras, making LiDAR-Camera Cross-modal Gait recognition (LCCGR) a critical yet challenging task due to the substantial modality gap between 2D videos and 3D point cloud sequences. To address this challenge, we propose TCFDNet, a Text-guided Cross-modal Feature Disentanglement Network, which leverages modality-aware textual priors as semantic anchors to guide the learning of disentangled modality-shared representations. Specifically, we construct a Gait Modality Text Dictionary (GMTD) using large language models to generate rich semantic descriptions of gait across modalities and viewpoints. A CLIP-based Multi-grained Feature Encoder then aligns visual and textual features within a unified vision-language space. Furthermore, the Text-guided Feature Disentanglement (TFD) module selects the topk matched textual descriptions to reconstruct modality-specific representations and derive modality-shared features via residual decomposition and orthogonality constraints. To mitigate the fragility of the disentangled shared features, we propose a Feature Stability Enhancement (FSE) module, which models spatial and channel-wise correlations to improve feature robustness. In addition, a cross-modal patch exchange strategy is introduced to further improve generalization. Extensive experiments on SUSTech1K and FreeGait datasets demonstrate that TCFDNet achieves new state-of-the-art results and validate the effectiveness of the proposed modules.

AI.tldr: TL;DR: 这篇论文用大语言模型生成的步态文本描述作为跨模态语义锚点，把 LiDAR 与相机步态特征解耦为共享与特有部分，并通过稳定性增强进一步提升鲁棒性，从而实现更强的 LiDAR-Camera 跨模态步态识别。 / TL;DR: The paper uses LLM-generated gait text descriptions as semantic anchors to disentangle LiDAR-camera gait features into shared and specific components, then strengthens the shared features for robustness, leading to stronger cross-modal gait recognition.
AI.motivation: 动机在于真实场景中的步态识别常同时涉及 LiDAR 和 RGB camera 等异构传感器，而 2D 视频与 3D 点云之间存在显著模态差异，导致跨模态步态识别困难；作者希望利用文本这一语义中介为跨模态表示学习提供稳定的共享锚点。 / The motivation is that real-world gait recognition often involves heterogeneous sensors such as LiDAR and RGB cameras, where the large gap between 2D videos and 3D point clouds makes cross-modal recognition difficult; the paper uses text as a semantic bridge to provide stable anchors for shared representation learning.
AI.method: 方法上，论文构建了由大语言模型生成的步态模态文本词典 GMTD，并使用基于 CLIP 的多粒度特征编码器将视觉与文本映射到统一空间；随后通过 TFD 模块选取 top-k 文本描述来重建模态特有特征，并以残差分解和正交约束提取模态共享特征；最后结合 FSE 模块增强共享特征稳定性，并引入跨模态 patch exchange 提升泛化。 / The method builds a gait modality text dictionary (GMTD) with LLM-generated descriptions, aligns visual and textual features via a CLIP-based multi-grained encoder, disentangles modality-specific and modality-shared features using the TFD module with top-k text matching, residual decomposition, and orthogonality constraints, then improves robustness with FSE and generalization with cross-modal patch exchange.
AI.result: 实验结果表明，TCFDNet 在 SUSTech1K 和 FreeGait 数据集上取得了最优性能，且消融实验验证了 GMTD、TFD、FSE 与 patch exchange 等模块的有效性。 / Results show that TCFDNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on SUSTech1K and FreeGait, and ablation studies confirm the contribution of GMTD, TFD, FSE, and patch exchange.
AI.conclusion: 提出的 TCFDNet 通过文本引导的跨模态特征解耦、特征稳定性增强以及跨模态 patch 交换，有效缩小了 LiDAR 与 Camera gait 表征之间的模态鸿沟，并在 SUSTech1K 与 FreeGait 上达到新的 SOTA。 / The paper concludes that TCFDNet effectively narrows the modality gap between LiDAR and camera gait data through text-guided disentanglement, feature stability enhancement, and cross-modal patch exchange, achieving new state-of-the-art results on SUSTech1K and FreeGait.

title: Diagnosing Failure Modes of Shared-State Collaboration in Resource-Constrained Visual Agents
summary: Modular visual reasoning systems increasingly rely on shared working memory for multi-step collaboration, yet the failure dynamics of intermediate state evolution in low-capacity regimes remain underexplored. We study failure modes of collaborative reasoning with weak learners (4B--8B models) through the lens of noise accumulation. We introduce CoSee, an auditing framework that formalizes the read-write-verify loop to trace information flow in document visual question answering. Across multi-page, chart, and web-based benchmarks, we find a counter-intuitive degradation: naive shared workspaces often amplify hallucinations rather than resolve them. We identify two dominant failure modes: Noise Reinforcement, where ungrounded notes are reused as evidence, and Policy Collapse, where added context shifts the model toward under-specified, short-form answers. Using cost-accuracy Pareto frontiers, we show that increased compute can correlate negatively with performance without explicit verification. Our findings suggest that for resource-constrained agents, the bottleneck lies not in reasoning depth but in communication fidelity, providing trace-level diagnostics and a mechanistic baseline for reliable modular design.

AI.tldr: CoSee shows that weak modular vision-language agents often fail because bad intermediate notes accumulate and get trusted. Shared memory without verification can make performance worse, not better, so reliable modular systems need explicit auditing and verification of communication.
AI.motivation: The motivation is that modular visual reasoning systems increasingly depend on shared working memory for multi-step collaboration, but the failure dynamics of intermediate state evolution under low-capacity settings are not well understood. The paper aims to explain why collaboration among weak learners can degrade rather than improve reasoning quality.
AI.method: The authors introduce CoSee, an auditing framework that models collaborative reasoning as a read-write-verify loop and traces how information propagates through shared intermediate states in document visual question answering. They evaluate weak learners (4B-8B models) on multi-page, chart, and web-based benchmarks, and analyze failures using cost-accuracy Pareto frontiers.
AI.result: The study finds a counter-intuitive performance degradation in naive shared workspaces: instead of correcting errors, collaboration often amplifies them. Two main failure modes are identified: Noise Reinforcement, where hallucinated notes are reused as evidence, and Policy Collapse, where extra context pushes models toward vague short answers. It also shows that more compute may correlate negatively with accuracy when verification is absent.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that in low-capacity modular visual reasoning systems, failures are driven more by poor communication fidelity in shared working memory than by insufficient reasoning depth. Without explicit verification, adding more compute or shared context can worsen performance by amplifying hallucinations and inducing underspecified answers.

title: Destruction is a General Strategy to Learn Generation; Diffusion's Strength is to Take it Seriously; Exploration is the Future
comment: Published April 27th, 2026 as an ICLR blogpost https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2026/blog/2026/destruction/
summary: I present diffusion models as part of a family of machine learning techniques that withhold information from a model's input and train it to guess the withheld information. I argue that diffusion's destroying approach to withholding is more flexible than typical hand-crafted information withholding techniques, providing a rich training playground that could be advantageous in some settings, notably data-scarce ones. I then address subtle issues that may arise when porting reinforcement learning techniques to the diffusion context, and wonder how such exploration problems could be addressed in more diffusion-native ways. I do not have definitive answers, but I do point my fingers in directions I deem interesting. A tutorial follows this thesis, expanding on the destroy-then-generate perspective. A novel kind of probabilistic graphical models is introduced to facilitate the tutorial's exposition.

AI.tldr: TL;DR：这篇论文不是提出一个具体更强的扩散算法，而是重新定义扩散模型的理解方式：把它看成“先隐藏/破坏信息，再训练模型恢复”的通用学习框架。作者认为扩散比传统手工遮蔽方法更灵活，可能更适合数据少的场景；同时提醒，把强化学习直接搬到扩散模型里会遇到探索问题，值得发展更“扩散原生”的解决方案。 / TL;DR: This paper does not mainly propose a stronger diffusion algorithm; instead, it reframes diffusion as a general destroy-and-recover learning paradigm. The author argues that diffusion’s destructive masking is more flexible than hand-crafted masking and may work especially well in low-data settings, while also highlighting unresolved exploration problems when reinforcement learning is adapted to diffusion and calling for more diffusion-native solutions.
AI.motivation: 动机在于重新理解扩散模型的本质，而不仅把它视为一种特定生成模型。作者希望说明：通过“破坏输入信息再恢复”的训练机制，扩散模型能够提供比传统手工遮蔽策略更丰富的学习环境，从而在某些场景，特别是数据稀缺场景中，带来优势。同时，随着强化学习与生成建模的结合增多，有必要澄清扩散框架下探索与训练信号设计的独特挑战。 / The motivation is to reinterpret diffusion models not merely as a specific generative model class but as a general information-withholding learning paradigm. The author aims to show that the destroy-and-recover mechanism creates a richer training playground than conventional hand-crafted masking approaches, potentially offering benefits in data-scarce regimes. A second motivation is to clarify the unique exploration and training-signal challenges that emerge when reinforcement learning ideas are adapted to diffusion models.
AI.method: 方法上，作者采用概念性与教程式分析：首先提出“先破坏、后生成（destroy-then-generate）”的统一视角来解释扩散模型；其次将扩散与其他信息隐藏式学习技术进行比较，强调其训练信号设计空间的灵活性；再次讨论强化学习方法迁移到扩散框架时的潜在问题；最后引入一种新的概率图模型表述来支持教程说明。 / Methodologically, the work is primarily conceptual and tutorial-driven: it introduces a unified destroy-then-generate perspective on diffusion, compares diffusion with other information-withholding learning techniques, analyzes issues that arise when porting reinforcement learning into the diffusion setting, and introduces a novel probabilistic graphical model formalism to support the exposition.
AI.result: 论文的主要结果不是一个新的SOTA算法，而是一个统一视角与研究议程：1）提出将扩散视为信息隐藏家族成员的理论框架；2）论证其“破坏式隐藏”具有更强灵活性；3）指出扩散与强化学习结合时存在尚未解决的探索问题；4）提供教程化解释，并引入新型概率图模型帮助理解。 / The main result is not a new state-of-the-art algorithm but a unifying perspective and research agenda: (1) framing diffusion as part of a broader information-withholding family, (2) arguing for the flexibility of destructive withholding, (3) identifying unresolved exploration issues at the diffusion–reinforcement learning interface, and (4) offering a tutorial supported by a novel probabilistic graphical model representation.
AI.conclusion: 该论文将扩散模型置于“隐藏部分信息并训练模型恢复被隐藏信息”的统一机器学习框架中，认为扩散式的信息破坏机制比手工设计的遮蔽策略更灵活，尤其可能在数据稀缺场景中更有价值。同时，作者指出将强化学习直接迁移到扩散建模会带来微妙的探索问题，现阶段没有定论，但提出了若干值得研究的方向。 / The paper places diffusion models within a broader family of learning methods that hide information and train models to recover it, arguing that diffusion’s destructive withholding mechanism is more flexible than hand-crafted masking schemes and may be especially useful in data-scarce settings. It also concludes that transferring reinforcement learning ideas into diffusion raises subtle exploration issues; while no definitive solution is given, several promising research directions are identified.

title: ElasticMem: Latent Memory as a Learnable Resource for LLM Agents
summary: Long-term memory is essential for LLM agents to reason coherently across extended interactions, personalize responses, and reuse past experience. However, existing memory-augmented methods typically treat memory as a fixed resource: text-space approaches concatenate retrieved memories into the context window, causing substantial token overhead and sensitivity to noisy evidence, while latent-space approaches reduce textual cost but still rely on rigid retrieval or fixed-capacity memory interfaces. This creates a mismatch between query-dependent memory utility and fixed memory allocation. We propose ElasticMem, a memory-augmented LLM framework that learns to use memory as an elastic latent resource. ElasticMem builds an offline latent memory bank with retrieval keys and content caches, retrieves memories adaptively from the reasoner's hidden state, assigns each retrieved memory a variable latent budget through a learned policy, and injects selected latent states as soft memory tokens for generation. The full memory-use process is optimized with downstream task rewards through group-relative policy optimization. We evaluate ElasticMem on MemorySuite, covering memory-intensive QA and embodied agent control. Across Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbones, ElasticMem improves weighted average QA accuracy by 26.2% and 24.6%, and improves ALFWorld success rate by 66.3% and 27.2%, respectively, over the strongest baselines, while achieving the lowest ALFWorld token cost. Ablations and qualitative analyses further show that adaptive retrieval and elastic budget allocation help ElasticMem prioritize useful evidence and transferable plans beyond rigid cosine similarity. Our code for ElasticMem will be released at https://github.com/ulab-uiuc/ElasticMem.

AI.tldr: ElasticMem lets an LLM use memory flexibly instead of allocating a fixed amount every time, leading to better QA and embodied-agent performance at lower token cost.
AI.motivation: Existing memory-augmented LLM methods allocate memory in a fixed way. Text-space methods incur heavy token overhead and are sensitive to noisy retrievals, while latent-space methods reduce textual cost but still use rigid retrieval or fixed-capacity interfaces. This mismatch between query-dependent memory utility and fixed memory allocation motivates a more adaptive memory mechanism.
AI.method: The paper proposes ElasticMem, which constructs an offline latent memory bank with retrieval keys and content caches, retrieves memories adaptively from the reasoner’s hidden state, allocates a variable latent budget to each retrieved memory via a learned policy, and injects selected latent states as soft memory tokens during generation. The memory-use process is trained with downstream task rewards using group-relative policy optimization.
AI.result: On MemorySuite, using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbones, ElasticMem improves weighted average QA accuracy by 26.2% and 24.6%, and improves ALFWorld success rate by 66.3% and 27.2% over the strongest baselines, while also achieving the lowest ALFWorld token cost. Ablation and qualitative studies show adaptive retrieval and elastic budget allocation better prioritize useful evidence and transferable plans.
AI.conclusion: ElasticMem demonstrates that treating memory as an elastic latent resource improves both effectiveness and efficiency for memory-augmented LLM agents. Adaptive retrieval and variable latent budget allocation outperform fixed memory allocation and rigid retrieval baselines.

title: MechVQA: Benchmarking and Enhancing Multimodal LLMs on Comprehensive Mechanical Drawing Understanding
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated significant achievements in general visual question answering (VQA) tasks. However, they remain brittle on mechanical engineering drawings, where high annotation density and weak domain knowledge, compounded by unreliable spatial relation reasoning under strict projection rules and geometric constraints, make decisive cues easy to miss and frequently lead to wrong answers. To bridge this gap, we introduce the first comprehensive mechanical drawing understanding dataset, MechVQA, created through a semi-automated construction and quality-control pipeline. MechVQA contains 3.3k high-density pictures with 21K question-answer pairs, spanning 10 different fine-grained tasks across three capability levels: Recognition, Reasoning, and Judging, providing a testbed to evaluate and improve MLLM understanding on real-world mechanical drawings. On top of MechVQA, we then develop the MechVL model through a multi-stage training paradigm, building a strong domain-specialized baseline. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that MechVL outperforms the strongest closed-source baseline by 7.57 percentage points on the MechVQA total score, significantly enhancing mechanical drawing understanding ability and providing a reusable foundation for deploying MLLMs in mechanical design and inspection scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MechVQA, the first large benchmark for mechanical drawing VQA, and MechVL, a specialized model trained on it; MechVL beats the best closed-source baseline by 7.57 points overall.
AI.motivation: General MLLMs perform well on broad VQA but are brittle on mechanical engineering drawings because these images have high annotation density, require domain knowledge, and demand reliable spatial reasoning under projection rules and geometric constraints.
AI.method: The paper builds MechVQA through a semi-automated construction and quality-control pipeline, organizing 3.3k dense mechanical drawings and 21K QA pairs into 10 fine-grained tasks across Recognition, Reasoning, and Judging. It then trains MechVL with a multi-stage training paradigm to create a strong domain-specialized baseline.
AI.result: MechVL outperforms the strongest closed-source baseline by 7.57 percentage points on the overall MechVQA score, showing significantly better understanding of mechanical drawings.
AI.conclusion: MechVQA provides the first comprehensive benchmark for mechanical drawing understanding, and the domain-specialized MechVL model substantially improves MLLM performance on this challenging domain, supporting practical deployment in mechanical design and inspection.

title: Learning to Adapt: Self-Improving Web Agent via Cognitive-Aware Exploration
summary: Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have led to promising progress in web agents. However, existing web agents often rely on handcrafted execution pipelines or expensive expert trajectories, limiting their adaptability to complex, dynamic environments. To address these challenges, we propose SCALE (Self-Cognitive-Aware Learning and Exploration), which leverages three adversarial roles, Selector, Predictor, and Judger to autonomously discover the agent's limitations and expand its cognitive boundaries through environmental exploration. Moreover, we propose SCALE-Hop, a graph exploration strategy that facilitates global planning and helps agents avoid local exploration traps. To further support learning, we construct SCALE-20k, a large-scale dataset collected from 19 real-world websites, containing diverse task types and structured demonstrations generated from SCALE's exploration traces. Experimental results show that our approach significantly improves the performance and generalization of multiple MLLMs in various web environments. Our framework offers a scalable and generalizable solution for building truly autonomous and adaptive web agents.

AI.tldr: 中文：SCALE 让网页智能体通过三个角色对抗式自我探索来发现短板，并结合图搜索和大规模真实网站数据集提升多模态模型在网页任务中的自主性、性能和泛化。 English: SCALE enables web agents to self-discover weaknesses through a three-role adversarial exploration framework, and combines graph-based planning with a large real-world dataset to improve autonomy, performance, and generalization on web tasks.
AI.motivation: 中文：现有网页智能体通常依赖手工设计的执行流水线或昂贵的专家轨迹，因此在复杂、动态网页环境中的适应性和扩展性不足。作者希望减少对人工规则和高成本标注的依赖，让智能体能够通过自主探索学习。 English: Existing web agents often depend on handcrafted pipelines or costly expert trajectories, which limits adaptability and scalability in complex, dynamic web environments. The motivation is to reduce reliance on manual engineering and expensive supervision by enabling agents to learn through autonomous exploration.
AI.method: 中文：论文提出 SCALE 框架，引入三个对抗性角色：Selector 用于选择探索目标，Predictor 用于预测结果与暴露能力边界，Judger 用于评估行为与反馈；三者协同促使智能体在环境中主动发现自身局限并持续学习。进一步提出 SCALE-Hop 图探索策略，用于全局规划并避免局部最优探索陷阱。同时构建 SCALE-20k 数据集，基于 19 个真实网站的探索轨迹生成结构化示范数据。 English: The paper proposes SCALE, a framework with three adversarial roles: Selector to choose exploration targets, Predictor to anticipate outcomes and reveal capability limits, and Judger to evaluate actions and feedback. Their interaction drives autonomous discovery of weaknesses and capability expansion. It also introduces SCALE-Hop, a graph exploration strategy for global planning and avoiding local traps, and builds the SCALE-20k dataset from exploration traces on 19 real-world websites.
AI.result: 中文：实验表明，SCALE 在多种网页环境中显著提升了多个多模态大模型的性能与泛化能力。SCALE-20k 也为训练和评估提供了大规模、多样化的数据支撑。 English: Experiments show that SCALE significantly improves the performance and generalization of multiple MLLMs across diverse web environments. SCALE-20k further supports learning with large-scale, diverse, and structured training data.
AI.conclusion: 中文：SCALE 通过自我认知驱动的探索、三角色对抗机制和图式跳跃搜索，能够在复杂网页环境中显著提升多模态大模型网页智能体的性能与泛化能力，是一种可扩展且通用的自主网页智能体框架。 English: SCALE improves the performance and generalization of MLLM-based web agents in complex web environments through self-cognition-driven exploration, a three-role adversarial mechanism, and graph-based hop exploration, providing a scalable and general framework for autonomous web agents.

title: Supervised Training Rapidly Degrades Early Visual Cortex Alignment Across Biologically Plausible Learning Rules
summary: Random, untrained neural networks consistently match or exceed trained networks in representational similarity to early visual cortex. This puzzling finding challenges the assumption that learning improves brain alignment. We investigate it by tracking representational similarity analysis (RSA) alignment to human fMRI data across training for four learning rules: backpropagation (BP), feedback alignment (FA), predictive coding (PC), and spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). Using 720 object images from the THINGS database and fMRI data from three subjects across six visual ROIs, we measure Spearman correlations between model and brain representational dissimilarity matrices at eight training checkpoints (epochs 0-40). We find that (1) a single epoch of training reduces V1 alignment by 25-90%, depending on the learning rule; (2) backpropagation reduces V1 alignment most severely (delta r = -0.080), while predictive coding and STDP preserve substantially more (delta r ~ -0.04); and (3) a weaker, opposite tendency appears in object-selective cortex (LOC), where BP shows the largest increase in alignment during training, although the absolute change is small. These results suggest that untrained architectures capture low-level visual statistics through inductive biases alone, and that global error signals (BP) reshape early representations more aggressively than local learning rules (PC, STDP), which better preserve brain-like structure.

AI.tldr: Training does not necessarily make networks more brain-like. Untrained networks already resemble early visual cortex, and learning, especially backpropagation, often damages that alignment. Local learning rules preserve early visual similarity better, while backpropagation slightly helps higher-level object cortex.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed that random, untrained networks can match or outperform trained networks in similarity to early visual cortex, which challenges the common assumption that learning improves brain alignment. The paper aims to explain how different learning rules change this alignment over training.
AI.method: The study tracks representational similarity analysis (RSA) between neural network representations and human fMRI responses during training. Four learning rules are compared: backpropagation, feedback alignment, predictive coding, and spike-timing-dependent plasticity. Using 720 THINGS images, fMRI data from 3 subjects, 6 visual ROIs, and 8 checkpoints from epochs 0 to 40, the authors compute Spearman correlations between model and brain representational dissimilarity matrices.
AI.result: After only one training epoch, V1 alignment drops by 25-90% depending on the learning rule. Backpropagation causes the largest V1 decrease (delta r = -0.080), while predictive coding and STDP show smaller drops (about -0.04). In object-selective LOC, the trend is weaker and partly reversed: backpropagation yields the largest increase in alignment, but the effect size is small.
AI.conclusion: Untrained architectures already align well with early visual cortex because their inductive biases capture low-level visual statistics. Training usually decreases V1 alignment, especially under global error-driven learning such as backpropagation, while more local rules like predictive coding and STDP preserve brain-like representational structure better.

title: SAGE: A Novelty Gate for Efficient Memory Evolution in Agentic LLMs
summary: Agentic LLMs must continuously decide whether newly extracted facts should be added, merged with existing memories, or ignored, yet prior work has focused more on retrieval and storage than on principled write-side control. We frame memory evolution as a novelty-detection problem and propose SAGE, a Spherical Adaptive Gate for memory Evolution that scores candidate facts with a von Mises-Fisher-based density estimator over memory embeddings and routes them with an adaptive threshold that tracks memory-store geometry. SAGE resolves clearly novel facts as ADD, clearly redundant facts as NOOP, and sends only uncertain cases to an LLM merge step, reducing expensive write-time reasoning. On LoCoMo, SAGE achieves the best average token-F1 against Mem0 on all seven open-weight backbone comparisons, while on GPT-4o-mini it reduces add-phase API cost by 3.4$\times$ and add-phase latency by 2.5$\times$ with only a small average judge-score gap. As a drop-in binary gate for A-Mem, SAGE skips roughly 16-18% of LLM calls across five models with minimal quality change on open-weight backbones. These results suggest that novelty-aware write control is a practical lever for improving both memory quality and system efficiency in long-term agentic memory.

AI.tldr: SAGE is a novelty-detection gate for agent memory writing: add novel facts, ignore redundant ones, and only ask an LLM to merge uncertain cases. It improves memory quality and significantly reduces write-time cost and latency.
AI.motivation: Prior work on agentic LLM memory has emphasized retrieval and storage, but has lacked principled control over whether newly extracted facts should be written, merged, or ignored. This creates inefficiency and unnecessary write-time reasoning costs.
AI.method: The paper formulates memory evolution as a novelty-detection problem and proposes SAGE, a Spherical Adaptive Gate for memory Evolution. It uses a von Mises-Fisher-based density estimator over memory embeddings to score candidate facts and an adaptive threshold based on memory-store geometry to route each fact to ADD, NOOP, or an LLM-based MERGE step.
AI.result: On LoCoMo, SAGE outperforms Mem0 in average token-F1 across seven open-weight backbones. On GPT-4o-mini, it cuts add-phase API cost by 3.4x and latency by 2.5x with only a small judge-score drop. As a binary gate for A-Mem, it avoids about 16-18% of LLM calls across five models with minimal quality impact on open-weight backbones.
AI.conclusion: SAGE demonstrates that novelty-aware write-side control can improve long-term agent memory systems by reducing unnecessary memory writes and expensive LLM merge operations while preserving or improving memory quality.

title: Function2Scene: 3D Indoor Scene Layout from Functional Specifications
summary: Most text-driven 3D indoor scene synthesis methods generate rooms from object-centric prompts, asking what furniture should be placed rather than how the space is used. Yet in real interior design, a layout is judged by how well it supports its occupants, e.g., their activities and physical needs. We introduce Function2Scene, a framework for generating 3D indoor layouts from functional specifications, i.e., natural-language design briefs describing who will use a room and what they need to do there. Given such a specification, our system parses occupant personas and activities, derives a customized set of functional design constraints from a taxonomy of 17 criteria spanning spatial, ergonomic, activity, and environmental considerations, and uses these constraints to guide layout generation. Rather than relying on an LLM to directly produce a final scene, Function2Scene performs iterative evaluation and refinement through a tool-augmented check-and-repair loop, combining geometric measurements, LLM-based contextual reasoning, and VLM-based visual assessment. Experiments on 30 professionally written interior-design cases show that Function2Scene produces layouts that better satisfy functional requirements than recent LLM-based scene synthesis baselines, with our results preferred in 94.3% of pairwise comparisons. Our work reframes text-driven indoor scene synthesis from placing plausible objects to designing spaces that support human use.

AI.tldr: Function2Scene turns text-based 3D room generation from object placement into function-aware interior design by extracting user needs and refining layouts with iterative constraint checking; it significantly outperforms prior LLM-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing text-driven 3D indoor scene synthesis methods focus on object-centric prompts about what furniture to place, but neglect whether the resulting space actually supports occupants’ activities, ergonomics, and practical needs.
AI.method: Function2Scene parses natural-language functional design briefs to identify occupant personas and activities, maps them to 17 functional design criteria, derives design constraints, and generates layouts through an iterative check-and-repair loop using geometric measurements, LLM reasoning, and VLM visual assessment.
AI.result: On 30 professionally written interior-design cases, Function2Scene outperforms recent LLM-based scene synthesis baselines in satisfying functional requirements, and its layouts are preferred in 94.3% of pairwise comparisons.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that indoor scene synthesis should be driven by functional human-use requirements rather than only object placement, and that an iterative constraint-guided generation loop produces more usable layouts.

title: HypoAgent: An Agentic Framework for Interactive Abductive Hypothesis Generation over Knowledge Graphs
summary: Abductive reasoning over knowledge graphs aims to generate logical hypotheses that explain observed entities or facts. Existing controllable hypothesis generation methods allow users to guide this process with explicit conditions, but they remain limited in interactive settings: they struggle to ground evolving natural-language intents across multi-turn dialogues and provide little fine-grained diagnosis when generated hypotheses fail. To address these limitations, we propose HypoAgent, an Agentic framework for interactive abductive Hypothesis Generation over knowledge graphs. HypoAgent integrates three agents: an Intent Recognition Agent that grounds user utterances and dialogue history into executable KG conditions, a Hypothesis Generation Agent that performs controllable hypothesis generation according to the extracted user intention, and a Root Cause Analysis Agent that diagnoses unreliable hypothesis fragments and leverages KG neighborhood probing to identify supported refinements. Experiments on commonsense and biomedical domain-specific knowledge graphs demonstrate that HypoAgent achieves state-of-the-art semantic similarity under single-turn, multi-turn, and unconditional settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/HKUST-KnowComp/HypoAgent.

AI.tldr: HypoAgent is a three-agent system for interactive KG-based abductive reasoning that understands evolving user intent, generates controllable hypotheses, and fixes weak parts, delivering state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Existing controllable hypothesis generation methods for knowledge graphs are not well suited for interactive use because they have difficulty grounding evolving natural-language intent in multi-turn dialogue and offer limited fine-grained diagnosis when generated hypotheses are unreliable.
AI.method: The paper proposes HypoAgent, an agentic framework with three components: an Intent Recognition Agent that converts multi-turn user utterances into executable KG conditions, a Hypothesis Generation Agent that generates hypotheses under those conditions, and a Root Cause Analysis Agent that diagnoses unsupported hypothesis fragments and refines them through KG neighborhood probing.
AI.result: On commonsense and biomedical knowledge graphs, HypoAgent outperforms prior methods and achieves state-of-the-art semantic similarity in single-turn, multi-turn, and unconditional hypothesis generation settings.
AI.conclusion: HypoAgent effectively enables interactive abductive hypothesis generation over knowledge graphs by combining intent grounding, controllable generation, and root-cause-based refinement, achieving state-of-the-art semantic similarity across multiple settings.

title: Zeroth-Order Non-Log-Concave Sampling with Variance Reduction and Applications to Inverse Problems
summary: Sampling from high-dimensional, non-log-concave distributions with unnormalized densities remains a fundamental challenge in machine learning, particularly in black-box settings where gradient information is inaccessible or computationally prohibitive. While Langevin dynamics provides a principled framework for sampling when gradients are accessible, its extension to the black-box settings suffers from high variance and lacks non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for non-log-concave sampling. To address these limitations, we propose a variance-reduced zeroth-order Langevin sampling method. Our method employs a gradient estimator that substantially reduces the variance of the classical batched zeroth-order estimator and eliminates the unfavorable dimensional dependence of the batch size required for accurate estimation, enabling practical and stable sampling. We establish the first non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for zeroth-order non-log-concave sampling in terms of $\varepsilon$-relative Fisher information, and, under a Poincaré inequality assumption, squared total variation distance. We further propose ZO-APMC, a posterior sampling algorithm for black-box inverse problems with pre-trained score-based generative priors, establishing the first non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for such methods. We validate our theory through synthetic experiments and demonstrate strong empirical performance on practical linear and nonlinear inverse problems.

AI.tldr: A new variance-reduced zeroth-order Langevin sampler enables more stable and practical black-box sampling for high-dimensional non-log-concave distributions, with the first non-asymptotic theory and strong results on inverse problems.
AI.motivation: The motivation is that sampling from high-dimensional, non-log-concave, unnormalized distributions is difficult in black-box settings where gradients are unavailable or too expensive. Existing zeroth-order extensions of Langevin dynamics suffer from high variance and lack non-asymptotic guarantees, especially for non-log-concave targets.
AI.method: The authors propose a variance-reduced zeroth-order Langevin sampling method using an improved gradient estimator with lower variance than classical batched zeroth-order estimators, while avoiding unfavorable dimension-dependent batch-size scaling. They also introduce ZO-APMC for posterior sampling in black-box inverse problems with pre-trained score-based generative priors.
AI.result: The paper establishes the first non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for zeroth-order non-log-concave sampling in epsilon-relative Fisher information and, under a Poincare inequality, squared total variation distance. It also proves the first such guarantees for posterior sampling with score-based generative priors in black-box inverse problems, supported by strong synthetic and practical inverse-problem experiments.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that variance-reduced zeroth-order Langevin sampling can make black-box sampling from high-dimensional non-log-concave distributions both theoretically tractable and practically effective. It provides the first non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for zeroth-order non-log-concave sampling and for black-box inverse-problem posterior sampling with score-based generative priors.

title: ExpGraph: Model-Agnostic Experience Learning with Graph-Structured Memory for LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown strong capabilities in reasoning, tool use, and multi-step interaction, but they often solve tasks from scratch and fail to reuse successful strategies or failure lessons from prior experience. Fine-tuning on collected experience can improve reuse, but it is inflexible when stronger or more suitable executors emerge. We propose ExpGraph, a model-agnostic experience learning framework that enables frozen and replaceable LLM executors to improve through external experience reuse without parameter updates. ExpGraph summarizes historical trajectories into reusable skills and failure lessons, organizes them as nodes in a self-evolving experience graph, and retrieves useful experiences through graph diffusion and utility-aware ranking. A lightweight retrieval copilot is trained with reinforcement learning using feedback that compares executor performance with and without retrieved experiences, while the graph is updated online from downstream task outcomes. We evaluate ExpGraph on ExpSuite, covering question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and multi-step agentic environments including ALFWorld and AppWorld. ExpGraph improves over the strongest baseline by 12.2% and 4.7% on static tasks with smaller and larger executors, and by 21.4% and 12.7% in agentic environments, while reducing average interaction steps by 12.7% and 21.6%. Ablations show that graph-structured experience, utility-aware ranking, and adaptive retrieval jointly enable effective experience reuse across diverse tasks and executor models.

AI.tldr: ExpGraph lets unchanged LLM agents get better by storing past successes and failures in an experience graph and retrieving the most useful lessons at inference time, producing clear gains across reasoning and agent tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents often repeatedly solve tasks from scratch and do not effectively reuse prior successful strategies or failures. Although fine-tuning can help, it is rigid when the executor model changes. The paper aims to enable flexible, executor-agnostic experience reuse without parameter updates.
AI.method: The paper proposes ExpGraph, a model-agnostic framework that converts historical agent trajectories into reusable skills and failure lessons, stores them as nodes in a self-evolving experience graph, retrieves relevant experience through graph diffusion and utility-aware ranking, trains a lightweight retrieval copilot with reinforcement learning based on performance differences with versus without retrieved experience, and updates the graph online from downstream outcomes.
AI.result: On ExpSuite spanning QA, math reasoning, code generation, ALFWorld, and AppWorld, ExpGraph outperforms the strongest baseline by 12.2% and 4.7% on static tasks with smaller and larger executors, and by 21.4% and 12.7% in agentic environments, while reducing average interaction steps by 12.7% and 21.6%. Ablations show graph-structured experience, utility-aware ranking, and adaptive retrieval are all important.
AI.conclusion: ExpGraph demonstrates that frozen, replaceable LLM agents can substantially improve performance by reusing externalized experience without fine-tuning, and that graph-based organization plus adaptive retrieval is an effective mechanism for cross-task experience transfer.

title: LegSegNet: A Public Deep Learning System for Lower Extremity CT Tissue Segmentation and Quantification
summary: Lower extremity computed tomography (CT) contains clinically relevant information for body composition analysis, sarcopenia assessment, and musculoskeletal disease monitoring, but extracting these measurements at scale requires accurate tissue segmentation and an automated quantification workflow. Existing public segmentation tools are not designed for comprehensive lower extremity CT analysis, particularly for clinically important inter/intramuscular adipose tissue, and most public methods only provide mask prediction rather than an end-to-end quantification system. To address this problem, we present LegSegNet, a deep learning system for lower extremity CT tissue segmentation and body composition quantification. Given an input CT scan, LegSegNet segments bone, skeletal muscle, subcutaneous adipose tissue, and inter/intramuscular adipose tissue. It then computes quantitative tissue measurements for downstream analysis. We developed the segmentation model using 1,302 manually annotated CT slices and evaluated it on 900 held-out test slices, with all annotations reviewed by radiologists. We benchmark LegSegNet against a broad set of 2D segmentation methods, including CNN-based models, transformer-based models, and finetuned foundation models, and further evaluate its generalization on an external public CT dataset. LegSegNet achieves the best overall segmentation performance, with an average Dice score of 89.31 on the held-out test set. To our knowledge, LegSegNet is the first publicly available end-to-end system for lower extremity CT tissue segmentation and quantification, providing a practical evaluation tool for future computer vision research in medical image analysis. The code and model weights are available at: https://github.com/mazurowski-lab/LegSegNet

AI.tldr: LegSegNet is a deep learning system that automatically segments multiple lower extremity tissues from CT and outputs quantitative body composition measurements; it outperforms strong baseline models and is released publicly as an end-to-end tool.
AI.motivation: Lower extremity CT contains important information for body composition analysis, sarcopenia assessment, and musculoskeletal disease monitoring, but existing public tools do not support comprehensive lower extremity tissue segmentation, especially inter/intramuscular adipose tissue, and usually lack an end-to-end quantification workflow.
AI.method: The paper proposes LegSegNet, a deep learning pipeline that takes lower extremity CT scans as input, segments bone, skeletal muscle, subcutaneous adipose tissue, and inter/intramuscular adipose tissue, and then computes quantitative tissue measurements. The model was trained on 1,302 manually annotated CT slices and evaluated on 900 held-out test slices, with annotations reviewed by radiologists. It was compared against multiple 2D CNN-based, transformer-based, and finetuned foundation segmentation models, and also tested on an external public CT dataset.
AI.result: LegSegNet achieved the best overall segmentation performance among compared methods, reaching an average Dice score of 89.31 on the held-out test set and demonstrating generalization on an external public CT dataset.
AI.conclusion: LegSegNet is the first publicly available end-to-end system for lower extremity CT tissue segmentation and quantitative body composition analysis, achieving state-of-the-art performance and practical utility for medical image analysis research.

title: FAM-Bench: A Multimodal Benchmark for Condition-Aware Food-as-Medicine Reasoning
summary: Food-as-Medicine requires models to reason beyond what a dish is or what nutrition it contains: they must decide whether a concrete food choice is appropriate for a specific health condition. Existing food AI benchmarks primarily evaluate dish recognition, recipe understanding, nutrient estimation, or general nutrition question answering, leaving this health-aware decision layer largely untested. We introduce FAM-Bench, a multi-modal Food-as-Medicine benchmark with 2500 nutrition-expert-verified instances across 13 diet-related health conditions. The benchmark contains two complementary tasks: dish-level suitability assessment, where models judge whether a dish is suitable for a condition from its image and ingredient list, and comparative dish analysis, where models rank four candidate dishes by condition-specific suitability. Both tasks require integrating ingredient evidence, visual preparation cues, and clinical nutrition constraints, providing a standardized testbed for grounded health-aware reasoning in language and vision-language models.

AI.tldr: This paper presents FAM-Bench, a new expert-verified multimodal benchmark for testing whether AI can judge which foods are suitable for specific health conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing food AI benchmarks focus on recognition, recipes, nutrient estimation, or general nutrition QA, but do not adequately test health-aware decision-making about whether a specific dish is appropriate for a specific medical or diet-related condition.
AI.method: The paper introduces FAM-Bench, a multimodal benchmark with 2,500 nutrition-expert-verified examples spanning 13 diet-related health conditions. It includes two tasks: dish-level suitability assessment using dish images and ingredient lists, and comparative dish analysis that ranks four dishes by suitability for a given condition.
AI.result: The main outcome is the creation of a standardized benchmark designed to evaluate grounded health-aware reasoning in language and vision-language models by combining ingredient evidence, visual preparation cues, and clinical nutrition constraints.
AI.conclusion: FAM-Bench fills a key evaluation gap by testing whether AI models can make condition-specific food suitability judgments, rather than only recognizing dishes or estimating nutrition.

title: Neuron-Level Interventions for Gendered and Gender-Neutral Generation in Language Models
summary: Language models (LMs) can produce gendered language and stereotypes even when given neutral prompts. Most prior work on gender bias in LMs primarily examines gender through a binary lens (feminine vs. masculine), with limited attention to gender-neutral forms, such as they/them pronouns or neutrally phrased job titles. How gender-related signals are encoded in the internal representations of LMs remains an open question. In this work, we study gender-specific neurons in LMs across three categories: feminine, masculine, and gender-neutral. We propose a neuron-level intervention method to identify neurons that are strongly tied to each gender category. We then test these neurons through controlled generation, showing that activating or masking gender-related neurons can steer a sentence toward a target gender form while preserving its original meaning. To evaluate the effectiveness of our gender-intervention approach, we curate two datasets with controlled sentences labeled across all three gender categories and validate the data quality through human evaluation. Experiments on two open-source LMs show that gender-specific neurons are not evenly distributed across model layers; instead, they concentrate heavily in the earliest layers with smaller contributions from later layers. Compared to existing methods, our method achieves more precise gender control, with less leakage into non-target gender categories and stable output quality through two evaluation criteria. Overall, our work examines how gender is encoded in LMs and provides a simple yet effective approach toward controlled gender intervention for both neuron intervention evaluation and gender bias mitigation. Code and datasets are available at: https://github.com/zhiwenyou103/Gender-Neuron-Intervention

AI.tldr: This paper finds and manipulates neurons tied to feminine, masculine, and gender-neutral language in LMs. By activating or masking those neurons, the model can steer outputs toward a target gender form with better precision and less leakage than prior methods, while revealing that most gender-related neurons cluster in early layers.
AI.motivation: Prior work on gender bias in language models mainly treats gender as a binary distinction and pays limited attention to gender-neutral expressions. The paper is motivated by the need to understand how broader gender signals, including neutral forms, are represented inside language models and how these signals can be controlled for analysis and bias mitigation.
AI.method: The authors propose a neuron-level intervention method to identify neurons strongly associated with three gender categories: feminine, masculine, and gender-neutral. They curate two controlled datasets labeled by gender category, validate them with human evaluation, and test interventions on two open-source language models through controlled generation by activating or masking the identified neurons.
AI.result: Experiments show that gender-specific neurons are unevenly distributed across layers and are concentrated heavily in the earliest layers, with smaller contributions from later layers. The proposed method achieves more precise gender control than prior approaches, reduces leakage into non-target gender categories, and maintains stable output quality under two evaluation criteria.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that gender-related information in language models is encoded in a sparse, layer-dependent set of neurons, concentrated mostly in early layers, and that targeted neuron activation or masking can reliably steer outputs toward feminine, masculine, or gender-neutral forms while preserving semantics. This provides an effective mechanism for controlled generation and bias mitigation.

title: Count Anything
summary: Object counting remains fragmented across domain-specific datasets and task formulations, despite rapid progress in generalist vision models. Existing counting models are often tailored to scenarios such as crowds, vehicles, cells, crops, or remote-sensing objects, and thus struggle to generalize across categories, visual domains, object scales, and density distributions. In this paper, we study text-guided object counting across domains, where a model takes an image and a natural-language query as input and returns an instance-grounded set of target points whose cardinality gives the count. This formulation unifies category-conditioned counting with interpretable spatial localization. To support this setting, we construct CLOC, a Cross-domain Large-scale Object Counting dataset that reorganizes diverse public data sources into a unified benchmark. CLOC covers six visual domains: General Scene, Remote Sensing, Histopathology, Cellular Microscopy, Agriculture, and Microbiology, with about 220K images, 619 categories, and 15M object instances. Based on CLOC, we propose Count Anything, a generalist model for text-guided object counting. Unlike density-map-based methods, which dominate counting models, Count Anything adopts discrete instance points and performs dual-granularity instance enumeration. A Region-level Sparse Counter provides object-level anchors for large and sparse targets, while a Pixel-level Dense Counter handles small, crowded, and weakly bounded targets via dense point prediction. A point-centric supervision strategy enables learning from heterogeneous annotations, and Complementary Count Fusion combines both counters in a parameter-free manner. Extensive experiments show that Count Anything achieves strong accuracy and multi-domain generalization, outperforming existing open-world counting methods. Code is available at: https://github.com/Mengqi-Lei/count-anything.

AI.tldr: 中文：这篇论文把“按文本描述数目标”统一成一个跨领域任务，先建了大规模基准 CLOC，再提出双粒度点式计数模型 Count Anything，在多领域上比现有开放世界计数方法更准、更泛化。 English: The paper unifies text-guided object counting across domains, introduces the large-scale CLOC benchmark, and proposes the dual-granularity point-based model Count Anything, which is more accurate and generalizes better than prior open-world counting methods.
AI.motivation: 中文：现有目标计数研究长期按场景和数据集割裂，模型通常只适用于人群、车辆、细胞、农作物等特定领域，难以跨类别、跨视觉域、跨尺度和跨密度分布泛化。因此需要一种统一、可解释且可跨领域泛化的文本引导计数框架。 English: Existing counting research is fragmented by domain-specific datasets and task setups, with models typically specialized for crowds, vehicles, cells, crops, and similar scenarios, leading to poor generalization across categories, visual domains, scales, and density distributions. This motivates a unified, interpretable, cross-domain text-guided counting framework.
AI.method: 中文：方法上，模型输入图像和自然语言查询，输出与目标实例对应的点集，点数即计数结果。Count Anything 采用双粒度实例枚举：区域级稀疏计数器负责大目标和稀疏目标，像素级密集计数器负责小目标、拥挤目标和边界弱目标；再通过以点为中心的监督策略适配异构标注，并使用无参数的互补计数融合整合两类结果。 English: The method takes an image and a natural-language query and outputs an instance-grounded point set whose cardinality is the count. Count Anything uses dual-granularity instance enumeration: a region-level sparse counter for large and sparse objects, a pixel-level dense counter for small, crowded, or weakly bounded objects, point-centric supervision for heterogeneous annotations, and parameter-free complementary count fusion to combine both counters.
AI.result: 中文：CLOC 数据集覆盖六个视觉领域，约 22 万张图像、619 个类别和 1500 万个实例。基于该基准，Count Anything 在广泛实验中展现出强准确率和跨域泛化能力，并优于现有开放世界计数方法。 English: CLOC spans six visual domains with about 220K images, 619 categories, and 15M object instances. On this benchmark, Count Anything demonstrates strong accuracy and cross-domain generalization, outperforming existing open-world counting approaches in extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: 中文：论文提出了跨领域文本引导目标计数任务，构建了统一基准数据集 CLOC，并提出通用模型 Count Anything。实验表明该方法在多领域泛化和准确性上优于现有开放世界计数方法。 English: The paper introduces cross-domain text-guided object counting, builds the unified CLOC benchmark, and proposes the generalist model Count Anything. Experiments show stronger accuracy and multi-domain generalization than existing open-world counting methods.

title: Answer-Set-Programming-based Abstractions for Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted for publication at the 42nd International Conference on Logic Programming (ICLP 2026). To appear in Theory and Practice of Logic Programming (TPLP)
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) enables autonomous agents to learn policies from experience, but realistic problems often involve enormous state spaces, making learning and generalisation challenging. Abstraction and approximation are therefore essential. Relational Reinforcement Learning (RRL) offers a way to reason about objects and their relations, and the CARCASS framework by Martijn van Otterlo demonstrates how logical representations can model Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) in first-order domains. Originally implemented in Prolog, CARCASS leverages domain knowledge to create powerful abstractions. We explore Answer-Set Programming (ASP), which is a rich and, contrary to Prolog, fully declarative modelling language, to realise CARCASS abstractions. We evaluate our ASP-based implementation in case studies of two domains, viz. Blocks World and Minigrid. Our results indicate that CARCASS with ASP provides a promising approach to constructing abstractions for RL, especially when domain knowledge is available.

AI.tldr: The paper ports CARCASS from Prolog to ASP and shows, via Blocks World and Minigrid, that declarative logical abstractions can help RL handle large relational state spaces when domain knowledge is available.
AI.motivation: Standard reinforcement learning struggles with huge state spaces and poor generalisation in realistic settings. The work is motivated by the need for abstraction and by the potential of relational/logical representations to exploit object structure and domain knowledge more effectively.
AI.method: The paper reimplements the CARCASS framework, originally built in Prolog, in Answer-Set Programming (ASP) to model first-order MDP abstractions, and evaluates the approach through case studies in Blocks World and Minigrid.
AI.result: The ASP-based CARCASS implementation works in two benchmark-style domains, Blocks World and Minigrid, and the reported results suggest that ASP is a viable declarative alternative for constructing RL abstractions.
AI.conclusion: Using Answer-Set Programming to realise CARCASS-style abstractions is a promising method for reinforcement learning in first-order relational domains, particularly when useful domain knowledge is available.

title: Counterfactual Evaluation Reveals Hidden Capability Profiles in Clinical LLMs and Agents
comment: Accepted to RLEval @ ACM CAIS 2026 (Workshop on Methods and RL Environments for Evaluating AI Agents) and selected for an invited talk based on reviewer ratings. 4-page short paper + appendix
summary: Two clinical AI systems can score nearly identically on coverage-based rubrics yet behave radically differently when their patient inputs change: one updates its recommendations to match the new clinical signal, while the other produces the same output regardless. We introduce the Causal Sensitivity Score (CSS), a pre-registered interventional metric that mutates oncology tumor-board cases along five clinically meaningful dimensions - biomarker flips, prior-treatment failures, biomarker removals, surgery-status changes, and stage perturbations - and scores whether each model updates its recommendations in the pre-registered correct direction using a {0, 0.5, 1.0} scale. Benchmarked against the Consensus Match Score (CMS), a coverage-based weighted recall metric, six frontier models from three labs evaluated in single-shot inference across 224 cases rank in nearly opposite orders: all six models change rank, the CMS-worst model becomes CSS-best, and one upper-mid CMS model ranks last on CSS. We further surface a universal safety blind spot: every frontier model fails on surgery-status interventions (at most 17.2% CSS on Family D), a finding CMS does not expose. The metric also transfers to tool-using agents: in a ReAct-style experiment, tool use improves CSS for five of six models (+2.5 to +20.3 percentage points), yet the lowest-CSS model retrieves the same chart sections and still fails to update its recommendations - revealing a structural responsiveness deficit visible only under counterfactual evaluation. Cross-judge replication and three-rater medical-professional validation confirm the aggregate findings. Interventional pre-registered metrics like CSS complement coverage-based evaluation for clinical AI agents: they capture responsiveness that coverage metrics miss and offer a candidate dense reward signal for future agentic RL systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes CSS, a counterfactual/interventional metric for clinical AI that tests whether models change recommendations appropriately when patient factors change. On 224 oncology cases, CSS reverses CMS-based rankings and exposes safety failures, especially around surgery-status changes, showing that coverage alone is not enough to evaluate clinical AI behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing coverage-based clinical AI evaluation can assign similar scores to models that behave very differently under changed patient inputs. The authors aim to measure whether a model updates its recommendations in the correct causal direction when clinically meaningful case details are altered.
AI.method: The paper introduces the Causal Sensitivity Score (CSS), a pre-registered interventional metric that mutates oncology tumor-board cases along five clinically meaningful dimensions: biomarker flips, prior-treatment failures, biomarker removals, surgery-status changes, and stage perturbations. Six frontier models from three labs were evaluated on 224 cases in single-shot inference and compared against Consensus Match Score (CMS). The study also tests transfer to tool-using ReAct-style agents, with cross-judge replication and three-rater medical-professional validation.
AI.result: CSS and CMS produce nearly opposite model rankings: all six models change rank, the CMS-worst model becomes CSS-best, and one upper-mid CMS model ranks last on CSS. All frontier models show a major blind spot on surgery-status interventions, with at most 17.2% CSS on Family D. In tool-using settings, CSS improves for five of six models by 2.5 to 20.3 points, but the lowest-CSS model still retrieves the same chart sections and fails to update recommendations, indicating a structural responsiveness deficit.
AI.conclusion: Interventional, pre-registered evaluation with CSS reveals clinically important responsiveness differences that coverage-based metrics like CMS miss, including universal failures on surgery-status changes, and can serve as a complementary evaluation and potential dense reward signal for clinical AI agents and future RL systems.

title: Robust Dreamer: Deviation-Aware Latent Gaussian Memory for Action-Controlled AR Video Generation
summary: Frame-wise action-controlled image-to-video generation is a promising paradigm for interactive world simulation, where each control signal should elicit an immediate visual response. However, maintaining visual fidelity and 3D consistency over long autoregressive rollouts remains challenging. Existing 3D-aware methods often suffer from catastrophic drift due to two impediments: information loss from \textit{Latent--RGB Cycling}, where generated latents are repeatedly decoded to RGB and re-encoded for future conditioning, and the training--inference gap induced by the \textit{error-free hypothesis}, where clean training memory fails to match prediction-corrupted inference memory. To address these challenges, we present \textbf{Robust Dreamer}, a memory-augmented framework built around how to design 3D memory and how to use it robustly. First, we introduce \textbf{Latent Gaussian Memory}, which anchors diffusion latents inherited from the generation process to Gaussian primitives and recalls them via latent-space Gaussian splatting. This provides dense, geometry-aware, view-aligned conditioning while avoiding accumulated degradation from repeated VAE conversion. Second, we propose \textbf{Deviation Learning with Dynamic Deviation Archive}, which synthesizes rollout-induced latent deviations through a one-step approximation, stores them by autoregressive stage and denoising timestamp, and injects them into historical memory during training. This exposes the generator to realistic corrupted memory states and teaches internal correction before inference. Experiments on ScanNet, DL3DV, and OmniWorldGame demonstrate state-of-the-art long-horizon performance.

AI.tldr: 中文：这篇论文通过把视频生成记忆保留在潜空间并显式训练模型处理历史误差，解决了长时程动作可控视频生成中的漂移问题。 English: This paper reduces long-horizon drift in action-controlled video generation by keeping memory in latent space and explicitly training the model to handle corrupted historical memory.
AI.motivation: 中文：现有3D-aware 长视频生成方法在长时程自回归 rollout 中容易灾难性漂移，主要因为两点：反复解码/重编码造成的信息损失，以及训练阶段依赖干净记忆、推理阶段却面对受污染记忆的分布差异。 English: The motivation is that existing 3D-aware long-horizon generation methods suffer catastrophic drift during autoregressive rollouts due to two main issues: information loss from repeated decode/re-encode cycles and the mismatch between clean training memory and corrupted inference memory.
AI.method: 中文：方法包含两部分。1）Latent Gaussian Memory：将扩散潜变量锚定到高斯表示，并通过潜空间 Gaussian splatting 回忆历史记忆，避免 latent-RGB 循环带来的信息损失。2）Deviation Learning with Dynamic Deviation Archive：用一步近似合成 rollout 误差，在按自回归阶段与去噪时间步组织的档案中存储，并在训练时注入历史记忆，以缩小训练-推理差距。 English: The method has two core components. (1) Latent Gaussian Memory anchors diffusion latents to Gaussian primitives and retrieves them via latent-space Gaussian splatting, avoiding information loss from latent-RGB cycling. (2) Deviation Learning with a Dynamic Deviation Archive synthesizes rollout-induced errors with a one-step approximation, stores them by autoregressive stage and denoising timestep, and injects them into training memory to reduce the train-inference mismatch.
AI.result: 中文：在 ScanNet、DL3DV 和 OmniWorldGame 上，Robust Dreamer 展示了更强的长时程生成稳定性、视觉质量和3D一致性，并取得了最先进结果。 English: On ScanNet, DL3DV, and OmniWorldGame, Robust Dreamer delivers stronger long-horizon stability, visual quality, and 3D consistency, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: 中文：论文提出了 Robust Dreamer，通过潜变量高斯记忆与偏差学习，显著提升了长时程、自回归、动作可控图像到视频生成中的视觉保真度与3D一致性，并在多个数据集上达到SOTA。 English: The paper concludes that Robust Dreamer, combining latent Gaussian memory and deviation learning, substantially improves visual fidelity and 3D consistency in long-horizon autoregressive action-controlled image-to-video generation, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks.

title: AutoSci: A Memory-Centric Agentic System for the Full Scientific Research Lifecycle
summary: Scientific research has traditionally been human-intensive, requiring researchers to coordinate literature, ideas, experiments, manuscripts, and review responses across long project cycles. The rise of LLM-based scientific agents creates an opportunity to automate this process. Such a system must support the full research lifecycle, maintain structured persistent memory across projects, and improve its own research procedures over time. However, existing systems either partially satisfy or fail to satisfy these requirements, leaving a gap for a unified automated scientific research system. As a result, we present AutoSci, a memory-centric agentic system for the full scientific research lifecycle. AutoSci is organized around four modules. SciMem provides schema-governed research memory, separating Long-Term Knowledge Memory for reusable scientific knowledge from Active Research Memory for project-level artifacts such as ideas, experiments, manuscripts, and reviews. SciFlow executes a five-stage lifecycle from literature understanding to rebuttal through a harness that controls state, context, verification, feedback, and orchestration. SciDAG augments difficult skills with DAG-shaped multi-agent operators and reusable stage-specific templates. SciEvolve converts feedback signals from users, experiments, reviews, and external environments into versioned updates to SciMem organization, SciFlow skills, and SciDAG templates. Together, these modules make AutoSci a persistent research environment that can execute, remember, and evolve across research projects. The code repository is available at https://github.com/skyllwt/AutoSci.

AI.tldr: AutoSci is an end-to-end AI research agent framework with long-term memory, project memory, workflow control, multi-agent operators, and feedback-driven self-improvement.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based scientific agents do not jointly satisfy three key needs: full-lifecycle support, structured persistent memory across projects, and continual self-improvement of research procedures.
AI.method: The system is built from four modules: SciMem for structured persistent memory, SciFlow for a five-stage research workflow, SciDAG for DAG-based multi-agent skill augmentation and reusable templates, and SciEvolve for turning feedback into versioned system improvements.
AI.result: The paper presents AutoSci as an integrated automated research environment that can execute research tasks, store and reuse knowledge, and evolve its skills and templates over time; a code repository is provided.
AI.conclusion: AutoSci proposes a unified, memory-centric LLM agent system that covers the full scientific research lifecycle and can persist knowledge and improve itself across projects.

title: Learning Transferable Predictability Representations
summary: We study the problem of assigning a scalar score to a short trajectory window that reflects its position on an ordered continuum of predictability regimes, spanning structured deterministic dynamics to unstructured stochastic noise. Existing methods address deterministic-versus-stochastic discrimination within a single system and do not produce scores with a consistent numerical interpretation across systems. We formalize this as ordinal estimation over a five-level predictability ladder and identify a structural source of cross-system ambiguity: ranking supervision alone leaves the score coordinate unfixed up to a monotone reparameterization, which we term the gauge freedom of ordinal scoring. We propose the Gauge-Fixed Ordinal Network (GON), a temporal convolutional model trained with an anchor-and-variance objective that pins level-wise score means to shared target coordinates. GON operates on 2-jet features that expose local trajectory geometry, preserved by smooth flows and disrupted by stochastic surrogate procedures. On five held-out dynamical systems, initializing from a pretrained GON checkpoint consistently outperforms training from scratch across all window budgets, with adaptation depth reflecting geometric proximity to the training family. Zero-shot scores retain ordinal structure at the stochastic boundary, where surrogate procedures most strongly disrupt nonlinear geometry, and pretrained initialization consistently beats scratch across all window budgets. Pairwise discrimination and globally coherent ordinal scoring are distinct properties requiring a stable score coordinate for cross-system transfer, with direct implications for predictability assessment, model selection, and early-warning diagnostics across natural and engineered dynamical systems.

AI.tldr: This paper builds a transferable predictability score for short dynamical trajectories. Its key insight is that ranking alone cannot define a shared score scale across systems, so it fixes that ambiguity with anchored ordinal training. The resulting GON model, using local geometric 2-jet features, transfers better, adapts faster, and gives more coherent cross-system predictability scores than scratch-trained baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing deterministic-versus-stochastic classifiers work mainly within a single system and lack a score with consistent meaning across systems. The paper is motivated by the need for a transferable scalar predictability score that can place short trajectory windows on a shared continuum from deterministic structure to stochastic noise.
AI.method: The method formulates predictability assessment as five-level ordinal estimation. It identifies monotone reparameterization ambiguity ('gauge freedom') in standard ordinal supervision, then introduces GON, a temporal convolutional network trained with an anchor-and-variance objective to align score means to shared coordinates across levels. The model uses 2-jet features to capture local trajectory geometry.
AI.result: On five held-out dynamical systems, pretrained GON initialization consistently outperforms training from scratch across all window budgets. Zero-shot scores preserve ordinal structure near the stochastic boundary, and adaptation depth correlates with geometric similarity to the training systems.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that globally coherent ordinal predictability scoring across different dynamical systems requires fixing the score coordinate, not just learning pairwise ranking. The proposed Gauge-Fixed Ordinal Network (GON) achieves this and improves transfer, zero-shot behavior, and low-data adaptation compared with training from scratch.

title: MosaicLeaks:Privacy Risks in Querying-in-the-Open for Deep Research Agents
summary: Deep research agents increasingly combine private local documents with external tools like web retrieval, creating a privacy risk: an agent's external queries may leak sensitive information from its local context. This risk is amplified by the mosaic effect, where individual queries may appear harmless but become revealing in aggregate. We introduce MosaicLeaks, a benchmark of 1,001 multi-hop deep research tasks that chain private enterprise documents and a public web corpus, forcing agents to make external queries that depend on local information. We evaluate leakage with an adversary LLM that observes only the agent's external queries and attempts to infer private information at three levels: the agent's research intent, answers to specific private questions and verifiable claims about the enterprise documents. We find that models across families and sizes frequently leak at all three levels, that zero-shot privacy prompting reduces but does not eliminate leakage and that reinforcement learning for task performance alone worsens leakage. To address this, we propose Privacy-Aware Deep Research (PA-DR), an RL framework that combines situational rewards for task success with a learned privacy classifier to provide dense credit assignment over both per-query and mosaic-level leakage. Training Qwen3-4B-Instruct with PA-DR improves accuracy from 48.7% to 58.7% and reduces answer and full-information leakage from 34.0% to 9.9%.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a benchmark for measuring how deep research agents leak private enterprise information through external queries and shows the problem is widespread. It then introduces a privacy-aware RL method, PA-DR, which both improves research accuracy and sharply reduces leakage.
AI.motivation: Deep research agents often use private local documents together with external web retrieval, which creates a risk that external queries leak sensitive local information. This problem is especially serious because the mosaic effect allows multiple individually benign queries to reveal private information when combined.
AI.method: The paper introduces MosaicLeaks, a benchmark of 1,001 multi-hop deep research tasks combining private enterprise documents with a public web corpus, and evaluates privacy leakage using an adversarial LLM that only sees the agent’s external queries. It then proposes Privacy-Aware Deep Research (PA-DR), a reinforcement learning framework that jointly optimizes task success and privacy via situational rewards plus a learned privacy classifier that provides dense feedback at both per-query and aggregate mosaic levels.
AI.result: Across model families and sizes, agents frequently leak private information at the levels of research intent, answers to private questions, and verifiable claims. Zero-shot privacy prompting reduces leakage but does not remove it, and reinforcement learning focused only on task performance makes leakage worse. PA-DR training on Qwen3-4B-Instruct improves accuracy from 48.7% to 58.7% and reduces answer/full-information leakage from 34.0% to 9.9%.
AI.conclusion: PA-DR can substantially reduce privacy leakage in deep research agents while improving task accuracy, showing that privacy-aware reinforcement learning is more effective than zero-shot prompting and avoids the leakage increase caused by optimizing only for task performance.

title: LinTree: Improving LLM Reasoning with Explicitly Structured Search Histories
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often solve reasoning problems by generating intermediate traces that explore and revise partial solutions. From a search perspective, these traces can be viewed as linearized search trees, where the model extends a partial solution, abandons it when it fails, and backtracks to try alternatives. Compared with traditional heuristic-guided search, such a policy has a potential advantage: it conditions on the whole search trace rather than only on the current local state. We first test whether LLMs utilize this advantage by comparing trace-conditioned reasoning policies against best-first search equipped with an LLM heuristic that only observes the current local state. Across three controlled reasoning environments, Blocks World, grid Navigation, and Sokoban, we find that raw access to search history alone is not enough to reliably outperform heuristic search. We then study one possible reason: in LLM reasoning traces, the underlying search tree is only implicitly represented, and when the model backtracks or switches branches, the trace does not explicitly identify which earlier search state is being revisited. We show that adding simple parent pointers to explicitly represent the linearized tree (LinTree) structure improves both task performance and search efficiency relative to implicit reasoning models and LLM-heuristic-guided search. These results suggest that search history becomes most useful when its tree structure is made explicit, motivating more structure-aware representations for LLM reasoning.

AI.tldr: LLMs do not automatically benefit from seeing their whole reasoning history; they benefit when that history is organized as an explicit tree. LinTree, a simple parent-pointer representation, outperforms implicit traces and heuristic search on several reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM reasoning often resembles search with backtracking over partial solutions. The authors investigate whether conditioning on the entire search trace gives LLMs an advantage over traditional heuristic-guided search, and whether failures stem from the fact that the underlying search tree is only implicitly encoded in ordinary reasoning traces.
AI.method: The paper compares three reasoning/search setups across controlled environments: trace-conditioned LLM policies that see full reasoning history, best-first search with an LLM heuristic that only sees the current local state, and an enhanced trace representation called LinTree that adds explicit parent pointers to linearized reasoning traces. Experiments are conducted in Blocks World, grid Navigation, and Sokoban.
AI.result: Full access to raw search history alone does not reliably beat heuristic search. However, when the trace explicitly encodes tree structure through parent pointers, LinTree yields better task success and higher search efficiency than both implicit reasoning traces and LLM-heuristic-guided search.
AI.conclusion: Making the search-tree structure explicit in LLM reasoning traces, via simple parent pointers (LinTree), improves both task performance and search efficiency compared with implicit trace-based reasoning and LAG heuristic search.

title: Efficient Diffusion LLMs via Temporal-Spatial Parallel Decoding and Confidence Extrapolation
summary: Diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) support parallel text generation via iterative denoising, yet inference remains latency-heavy because many steps are spent on redundant refinement and repeated remasking of tokens whose final values are already determined. Prior acceleration methods mainly depend on step-local confidence heuristics or fixed schedules, which are sensitive to prompt and task variation and ignore strong positional effects within a sequence. We cast diffusion decoding as a dynamic control problem and show that token-wise denoising trajectories provide the key signal for reliable control. We propose a trace-aware decoding framework with two components. First, Temporal-Spatial Parallel Decoding (TSPD) uses a lightweight temporalspatial controller that consumes per-token trajectory features, including confidence, entropy, and momentum, together with token position, to decide when a token has converged and can be safely fixed.
